articles.title: US issues fresh sanctions against individuals and entities aiding Iran
articles.description:
US issues fresh sanctions against individuals and entities aiding Iran

    
    

        
    
                The US Treasury issued fresh sanctions on Wednesday targeting what it called "the vast criminal network" of companies and individuals tied to Iran.

It named Indian nationals Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, as well as two other Indian citizens who head two of the couple's businesses, and nine separate entities connected to Sharma.

"Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies," the department said in a statement.

The department also sanctioned Turkey-based Fugo Group Services Inc for its ongoing support of Iran's heavily sanctioned aviation sector.

articles.title: 'I think a part of it was Iran': Trump acknowledges war's impact on midterm election losses
articles.description:
'I think a part of it was Iran': Trump acknowledges war's impact on midterm election losses

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 10:21

        
      
    
      
    
                The prices of goods and petrol have risen in the US as a direct result of the unpopular war in Iran, and played a role in the Democrats gaining control of the Senate and House of Representatives
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US President Donald Trump speaks during a round table at the White House in Washington, DC, US, 21 October 2026 (Kevin Lamarque/ Reuters)
                  Off
                  US President Donald Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the war on Iran played a part in the Republican party’s sweeping midterm election losses. 

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, with politicians who had campaigned on their opposition to the war scoring notable victories.

In separate interviews reflecting on the reasons behind his party’s heavy defeats, Trump said: “I think a part of it was Iran… Iran was a piece of it.”

Nevertheless, the US president stood by his decision to join Israel in attacking Iran, which also went against the “no new wars” messaging of his 2024 presidential campaign.

“I did the right thing,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal. “I would have done it again.”
  
    



  



The US and Israel went to war with Iran at the end of February, after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly presented Trump with intelligence from Mossad convincing him that doing so would lead the Iranian people to rise up and overthrow their government. 

Cost of living

But despite killing a slew of Iranian leaders, including former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, the government in Tehran has remained intact and the Iranian military has seized control of the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices skyrocketing across the globe.  

The attendant rise in the cost of petrol and other goods at home in the US was a theme of the Democrats’ messaging, with candidates across the country blaming the war for the high cost of living.

Trump has chopped and changed his stated priorities for the war, which has remained consistently unpopular with Americans. 

Asked after the midterm results about reports that he was considering using a nuclear weapon on Iran, Trump said: “I don’t need it, we’ve knocked them out already, 90 percent.”

In Tehran, the US election results were met with satisfaction. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Wednesday on X.

articles.description:
Trump admits Iran war caused election losses but ‘we had to do it’

    
    

        
    
                US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the Iran war was responsible for his Republican Party's resounding midterm election defeat.

Asked whether he agreed with Vice President JD Vance earlier remarks that the Iran war was "the reason we lost", Trump told reporters outside the White House ballroom construction site that his comments were "largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term".

"But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he added.

He also ruled out firing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying "he's doing a very good job," despite his role in pushing for military action against Tehran.

  
  
      



    US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before the construction site of the East Wing ballroom at the White House in Washington, DC, on 4 November 2026 (Mandel Ngan/AFP)

articles.title: UK: Dozens arrested outside Supreme Court hearing on Palestine Action ban
articles.description:
UK: Dozens arrested outside Supreme Court hearing on Palestine Action ban 

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Areeb Ullah
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 17:30

        
      
    
      
    
                Lawyers representing the co-founder of Palestine Action said the group follows the traditions of the Suffragette movement
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Dozens of activists, including Jewish activists, and celebrities faced arrest on first-day of last ditch appeal against ban on the direct-action group (Reuters)
                  Off
                  Lawyers representing the co-founder of Palestine Action have argued that the direct-action group has never advocated for violence against individuals as the campaign to overturn its designation as a terrorist organisation by the UK government reached the Supreme Court.

Speaking on the first day of the two-day hearing, Raza Husain KC, representing Huda Ammori, opened proceedings and said that less than one percent of the group’s protests met the legal definition of terrorism.

"It’s not the label that's important – it’s the substance. Palestine Action has never advocated violence against individuals and follow a similar vein to the Suffragettes who were not peaceful... are part of the tradition [and] proven right by history and venerated.

“The uncontroverted evidence shows moreover that [the] Suffragettes, anti-war groups, environmental groups, animal rights protesters all used tactics similar to or more extreme than Palestine Action, yet they were not regarded as terrorists or proscribed,” said Husain.

The barrister noted that the Suffragettes are now widely celebrated despite using tactics like arson and bomb attacks in the cause of campaigning for the right to vote for women.
  
    



  



Ammori’s legal team also emphasised that the ban on Palestine Action had impacted the group’s right to freedom of speech and protest, noting that it had created a “chilling effect” on British society.

“Filton marked a watershed moment - [the activists] were arrested as terrorists and treated as such,” said Husain.

“That came as a shock to the movement.”

The Supreme Court hearing comes after judges granted an appeal following the government's successful proscription under anti-terrorism laws.

It marks the final attempt for the group to appeal the ban after going through several courts to reach this stage.

Outside the court, dozens of activists risked arrest for holding signs that quoted posts from Sarah Helm, former journalist and wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who caused an uproar after publicly criticising the ban on Palestine Action.

Last month, Helm posted “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” after books by Irish author Sally Rooney were withdrawn from sale in the UK because of her support for the group.
  
    



  



Protesters customised the signs by swapping out “authors” for descriptors that reflected their personal identities or professions - including “Jew”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or “normal people”.

Among 25 people who were arrested by the police for holding the placards are actor Alfie Enoch, who starred in the Harry Potter movies, and Massive Attack musician Robert Del Naja.

articles.title: Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
Americans voted against war. The Democrats must not mistake that for a mandate
articles.description:
Americans voted against war. The Democrats must not mistake that for a mandate

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Omar Suleiman
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 17:20

        
      
    
      
    
                Midterms showed that political power can be challenged, even when backed by extraordinary wealth. But can this movement be channelled towards global peace?
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer takes questions in Washington, DC, on 4 November 2026, after historic Democratic midterm victories (Tom Brenner/Getty Images/AFP)
                  Off
                  The American political establishment is about to learn a dangerous lesson from the wrong interpretation of a historic election.

On Tuesday night, voters delivered a devastating rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his cronies, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the process. 

Candidates who challenged the political consensus around Israel, Gaza and Iran achieved victories that would have seemed unimaginable only a few years ago. 

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), long treated as an almost untouchable force in American electoral politics, watched candidates it opposed prevail, despite extraordinary spending. Association with Aipac and pro-Israel lobbying groups is now a liability. 

And before Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries congratulate themselves, they should understand something: the voters who made these victories possible did not vote for them and their Democratic establishment. In fact, they voted against it.
  
    



  



This was not simply a Democratic wave; it was a revolt against a political order that has made endless war a bipartisan commitment, Palestinian suffering an acceptable cost of doing business in the Middle East, and American taxpayers unwilling financiers of destruction abroad, while their own communities struggle at home with all sorts of avoidable challenges.

The results were not exclusively a referendum on foreign policy. Americans also voted against rising living costs, corruption and an increasingly unpopular president. 

But the Gaza genocide and the Iran war, launched at Israel’s behest, were no longer peripheral issues that candidates could safely avoid. They became part of a larger reckoning over what American power is being used for, who benefits from it, and who is expected to pay the price.

Historic victory

The question now is whether the Democratic Party will recognise that shift, or attempt to absorb the energy of an antiwar movement while preserving the very policies that made such a movement necessary. With the history of the Democratic Party, most of us aren’t holding our breath.

Abdul El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, defeated Republican Mike Rogers after surviving one of the most aggressive campaigns against a candidate in recent memory.

His victory was historic, of course. But reducing it to a milestone of religious representation would miss its political significance.

According to the Associated Press news agency, Aipac spent nearly $30m opposing him during the Democratic primary. Its preferred candidate, Representative Haley Stevens, lost.


The Democratic establishment cannot credibly present itself as the innocent beneficiary of public outrage. It helped create that outrage


Then, just two days before the election, Stevens endorsed Sayed’s Republican opponent, Rogers. After months of bitter disagreement over Israel and sabotaging her former opponent, she decided that defeating the Democratic nominee was preferable to accepting the direction Michigan voters had chosen.

It was an extraordinary exposure of the priorities operating within the party’s establishment.

Even though Schumer and others in the establishment leadership condemned the latest move by Stevens, and supported Sayed in Tuesday’s election, they had almost all backed Stevens during the primary, and were timid in their acceptance of Sayed even before the Stevens stunt. The establishment ultimately rallied behind the nominee only after voters had rejected its preferred choice.

The party leadership should not be allowed to rewrite the story as though it had enthusiastically nurtured the very movement it initially attempted to defeat.

Michigan voters were told, in effect, that a candidate willing to challenge unconditional support for Israel was too risky, too divisive and too far outside the political mainstream.

They elected him anyway. And Michigan was hardly alone. In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins after openly criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza and opposing unconditional American military assistance.
  
    



  



In Texas, James Talarico, who has spoken of his opposition to the Gaza slaughter from the perspective of a Christian and former teacher, won a Senate seat that Democrats had been unable to capture for more than three decades.

Framework shattered

Now, I want to say this clearly: I don’t believe any of these candidates have gone nearly as far as they should have in openly calling out Israel’s criminality, without somewhat pandering to the liberal Zionists stuck in the current Democratic ranks. But they have all gone further than what was typically acceptable in the political order.

And these candidates are not ideologically identical, nor did every Democratic victor campaign against Aipac. But their victories demonstrate that unconditional support for Israeli military policy is no longer the prerequisite for political viability that Washington once assumed.

The old threats are losing some of their power.


  

  Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
    Read More »


For decades, American politicians were conditioned to speak about Israel in a narrow vocabulary. Security was legitimate. Palestinian freedom was controversial.

The genocide in Gaza has shattered much of that framework. Americans watched hospitals destroyed, children pulled from rubble, journalists killed, and families displaced repeatedly. They watched their government continue supplying weapons, while insisting that it was working tirelessly for peace.

Under former President Joe Biden, the Democratic administration helped to sustain Israel’s military campaign, even as outrage grew over Palestinian civilian deaths. Under Trump, the Republican administration embraced further military escalation and deepened the regional catastrophe. Same garbage, different pile: that’s how many of us felt.

This is why the Democratic establishment cannot credibly present itself as the innocent beneficiary of public outrage. It helped create that outrage.

And the shift was visible well before election night. Polling reported by Al Jazeera in August showed substantial opposition to continued military aid to Israel among Democratic voters in early presidential primary states.

The distance between the party’s leadership and its voters has become impossible to ignore.

Moral rupture

The Israel lobby’s problem is therefore bigger than a series of electoral defeats. Its political brand has become increasingly associated with a foreign policy that many Americans no longer wish to defend.

That does not mean the organisation has lost its money, access or influence. It means those resources no longer guarantee political obedience.

And that is an important beginning. Gaza was the moral rupture, and the war on Iran widened the political reckoning.

  
  
      



    Abdul El-Sayed and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, take the stage after he won the Michigan Senate race, in Detroit, on 4 November 2026 (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP)
  




  
    



  











For years, Americans were told that each new military escalation in the Middle East would make them safer. Each intervention came with assurances of strategic necessity, limited objectives and eventual stability.

Yet Americans have watched the same repeated cycle, over and over again: military escalation, civilian suffering, regional instability, enormous public expenditures, and promises that the next use of force will finally deliver security.

The war on Iran just brought that contradiction home, especially for “America Firsters” who felt betrayed.

Voters facing rising prices and economic uncertainty were once again being asked to accept the costs of another foreign war. The administration that promised to put America first was consumed by military confrontation abroad.

Schumer and Jeffries may soon hold extraordinary institutional power. But the Democratic leadership’s record on Israel gives little reason to assume that electoral victory will produce meaningful change in that party.

Opportunities squandered

In April, Schumer was among a small minority of Senate Democrats who opposed resolutions seeking to block certain weapons sales to Israel. In July, Jeffries voted against ending American military aid, even as a substantial portion of his caucus supported the measure.

These were opportunities to use congressional power to challenge the material support sustaining Israeli military operations, and they squandered it again.

The leadership chose continuity, and now it will have fewer excuses. The problem is not that the Democratic Party lacks the means to pursue a different policy. It is that too many of its leaders have lacked the willingness to exercise a moral backbone. 


A true antiwar movement must be willing to support candidates who uphold those commitments, and challenge those who abandon them, no matter what party they come from


The deeper question is whether this election represents a temporary protest against Trump, or the beginning of a lasting transformation of American politics. I hope it is the latter, but I am very sceptical.

The US does not simply need Democrats who are more articulate in condemning Republican wars, while remaining willing to finance wars of their own. It needs a political movement that understands opposition to war as a governing principle, rather than a campaign slogan. That means opposing illegal and unnecessary military interventions, regardless of which party occupies the White House.

It means applying international law consistently, whether the accused government is an American adversary or a so-called ally.

It means challenging the military-industrial complex and the enormous political incentives that make war profitable for some, while catastrophic for millions.

And it means building an economic vision that recognises the connection between militarism abroad and neglected needs at home.

The path forward

A true antiwar movement must be willing to support candidates who uphold those commitments and challenge those who abandon them, no matter what party they come from. It must also refuse to disappear once the election is over.

Because the political establishment has a familiar way of surviving popular revolts. It adopts their language, celebrates their victories, and then quietly restores the policies that produced the revolt in the first place.

The Democrats cannot be permitted to do that with Gaza as it continues to bleed, as the genocide started and was sustained on their watch. They cannot be permitted to do that with this stupid war on Iran and what follows.

There is much to celebrate about Tuesday’s election, with some of the worst actors in modern political history being sent packing.


  

  Can Iran war deadlock be broken at the US ballot box?
    Read More »


Candidates who were told they could not win without submitting to the old foreign policy consensus proved otherwise. Communities that had been dismissed as politically expendable demonstrated their electoral power. A lobbying establishment accustomed to intimidating dissent discovered that voters could reject its preferred candidates.

Aipac’s defeats should not become merely another chapter in the Democratic Party’s comeback story. They should mark the beginning of the end of a bipartisan consensus that has wreaked havoc on so many innocent lives with our tax dollars for too many years to count.

If Schumer and Jeffries interpret this election as permission to restore the old order, they will have misunderstood the moment. If the antiwar movement interprets it as proof that its work is finished, it will have misunderstood the struggle. And if they return to business as usual, they should understand that they can lose their own primaries next time around.

The American people have demonstrated that political power can be challenged, even when backed by extraordinary wealth and institutional influence.

The next question is whether that power can be redirected towards peace.

The voters have opened a door that the political establishment spent decades trying to keep shut. Now the US needs an antiwar movement strong enough to make sure it never closes again.

articles.title: Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
articles.description:
Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island 

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 15:59

        
      
    
      
    
                US officials said they launched 'defensive' strikes on Qeshm Island, the same day Trump vowed not to attack Iran
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A picture taken on 30 April 2023 shows a general view of the Iranian island of Qeshm (Atta Kenare/AFP)
                  Off
                  Iran cast doubt on the chances of a deal with the US on Tuesday, after the US carried out air strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, with the fate of last-minute negotiations between the two sides uncertain.

The air strikes, which occurred late on Monday, came after US President Donald Trump said he did not plan to attack Iran after the midterm elections and voiced hope for a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said an agreement could be reached and that the government was “authorised” to renew a truce.

However, on Tuesday, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, rejected an offer passed to Tehran from Qatari negotiators.

“America’s response to the demands of the Iranian nation was insufficient. They must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened,” he said on X.

Last-minute negotiations to avert what officials and analysts in the region say could be a return to full-scale war took place against the backdrop of US air strikes on Qeshm Island, a strategic place that Iran has used as it attempts to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.
  
    



  



The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the strikes on Qeshm, said the US was deliberately keeping the attacks quiet to reduce the risk of escalation. One US official described the strikes as “defensive” in the report.

According to the report, in one exchange, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired a surface-to-air missile at a US warplane, which fired back in self-defence. Another strike occurred after the US intercepted a missile fired from Qeshm at a commercial vessel. 

Iran also said it downed a US MQ-9 Reaper drone and two Lucas drones near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. 


  

  Houthis launched cross border raids on Saudi military posts, sources say
    Read More »


Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after Tehran had delivered what he described as a "strong and rational response” to the proposal conveyed by Qatar.

"The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Tehran has a seven-step proposal for a diplomatic solution that could be implemented in two days.

The plan would call for the US to end its blockade on Iranian ports, Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz waterway, a US waiver on Iranian oil sales, the cancellation of new sanctions on Iran, and then talks on the nuclear file.

The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire in the spring and then signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding to advance talks, but it was never implemented. The talks collapsed in part over the US’s reluctance to agree to Iran controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: ‘It will crush us’: Israeli leaders in panic mode over fallout from US elections
articles.description:
‘It will crush us’: Israeli leaders in panic mode over fallout from US elections

    
    

        
    
                Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid warned after the US election results that Netanyahu’s continued leadership would endanger Israel’s security and deepen its international isolation.

"Israel cannot afford for him (Netanyahu), to remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world," Lapid wrote on X.

"The American election results in the morning have one unexpected outcome: they eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu," he added.

Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, also sounded the alarm, warning that Netanyahu’s continued rule could push an already internationally isolated Israel towards “international sanctions, international isolation and a collision with the United States”.

Jerusalem Post analyst Amichai Stein warned that the results could bring “harsher criticism of Israel, and less willingness to defend the traditional relationship between the two countries.”

articles.title: ‘Israel cannot afford to ignore’: Israeli press reels from Democratic sweep
articles.description:
‘Israel cannot afford to ignore’: Israeli press reels from Democratic sweep

    
    

        
    
                The Israeli press is taking stock of last night’s Democratic sweep of Congress, sounding the alarm over the consequences for Israel.

A Haaretz analysis this morning said Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over pro-Israel candidate Mike Rogers demonstrated “that even strident opposition to Israel is no barrier to winning competitive federal races.”

“El-Sayed won despite AIPAC spending more than $30 million to defeat him in the Democratic primary and another reported $9 million on behalf of Rogers in the general election,” it added.

The Jerusalem Post warned: “The implications of the US midterm elections for Israel could extend far beyond the loss of Republican control of Congress. The defeat comes amid broader shifts within the Democratic Party regarding Israel, the war with Iran, and the strategic relationship between Jerusalem and Washington.”

“One of the clearest takeaways from the election campaign is the political price the war with Iran has exacted on the Republican Party”, the analysis said, referring to the war Israel pushed the US into on 28 February.

“The expansion of the camp critical of Israel, and its growing access to positions of influence, represents a shift that Israel cannot afford to ignore,” it added.

articles.title: US election results fuel Israeli opposition's push to remove Netanyahu
articles.description:
US election results fuel Israeli opposition's push to remove Netanyahu

    
    

        
    
                As news emerged on Wednesday that the Democratic Party had won a landslide victory, regaining control of the US Congress, Israeli politicians, journalists and experts warned of the results' grave implications for Israel's national security, pointing to the declining standing of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the US.

Former Israeli prime minister Yair Lapid, who was re-elected to parliament last week as part of the centre-right Together alliance, said the US election results had "eliminated" any possibility of forming a unity government with Netanyahu.

"Israel cannot afford for him to remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world," Lapid said on X on Wednesday morning.

Recent Israeli reports indicated that US President Donald Trump is applying pressure on Netanyahu and the Israeli opposition leaders to form a unity government that will exclude extremists in order to advance his Middle Eastern policies.

Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats alliance, also described Netanyahu as a threat to Israel's security in the wake of the US election results, which saw progressive Democrats, including Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed – the first Muslim elected to the US Senate – win races across the country.

Read more: US election results fuel Israeli opposition's push to remove Netanyahu

articles.title: US election results fuel Israeli opposition's push to remove Netanyahu
articles.description:
US election results fuel Israeli opposition's push to remove Netanyahu

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Nadav Rapaport
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:32

        
      
    
      
    
                Israeli opposition leaders warn that the Democrats' sweep of US Congress could threaten Israel’s national security
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu gestures as he reacts to exit polls, at his party headquarters during Israel's national election, in Jerusalem, 28 October 2026 (Reuters)
                  Off
                  As news emerged on Wednesday that the Democratic Party had won a landslide victory, regaining control of the US Congress, Israeli politicians, journalists and experts warned of the results' grave implications for Israel's national security, pointing to the declining standing of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the US.

Former Israeli prime minister Yair Lapid, who was re-elected to parliament last week as part of the centre-right Together alliance, said the US election results had "eliminated" any possibility of forming a unity government with Netanyahu.

"Israel cannot afford for him to remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world," Lapid said on X on Wednesday morning.

Recent Israeli reports indicated that US President Donald Trump is applying pressure on Netanyahu and the Israeli opposition leaders to form a unity government that will exclude extremists in order to advance his Middle Eastern policies.

Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats alliance, also described Netanyahu as a threat to Israel's security in the wake of the US election results, which saw progressive Democrats, including Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed – the first Muslim elected to the US Senate – win races across the country.
  
    



  



Golan said Netanyahu has become "toxic" in the US, both within the Democratic party and the Republican party, adding that if the Israeli prime minister continues to rule it could "lead Israel onto a path of international sanctions, international isolation, and a collision with the United States".


'Netanyahu’s continued tenure is an immediate danger to our special relationship with the United States'

- Amir Tibon, Haaretz


According to Golan, the most left-leaning leader of the Zionist Israeli opposition, Israel is now facing a choice between a "boycotted, backward, and isolated" country led by Netanyahu, or "a strong, advanced, free, and secure Israel".

"Netanyahu lost the elections. He is dangerous to Israel," Golan said on X, adding "we have no time to waste. We must form a change government now."

The Democrats MP Gilad Kariv echoed the position of his party leader on Wednesday, ruling out a unity government with Netanyahu's Likud party.

Kariv said on X that "anyone who is still talking this morning about unity with Netanyahu does not understand the results of the elections in Israel and does not understand the results of the elections in the United States."

'US-Israel relations comes to an end'

Progressive US Democrats like Sayed, who have been calling for an end to military aid to Israel over its genocide in Gaza, are viewed by Israeli US affairs experts and journalists as a threat to Israel's very existence.

On Wednesday, former Israeli foreign minister Tzipi Livni, a fierce critic of Netanyahu, said that the prime minister can no longer "preserve the legitimacy of the existence of the state of the Jewish people, or our right to defend ourselves, in the face of the views of some of the newly elected officials".


'An era of half a century in US-Israel relations, as we have known it, comes to an end'

- Michael Oren, former Israeli diplomat


Gili Cohen, the diplomatic correspondent of Israel's Kan 11, said the US electoral results are "not only a defeat for President Donald Trump, but also for Israel’s standing" in the US, as the much-needed American military aid is now on the balance.

Amir Tibon, a journalist at the Israeli left-wing newspaper Haaretz, described the election results as "a political earthquake" with grave consequences for Israel.

"Netanyahu’s continued tenure is an immediate danger to our special relationship with the United States," he wrote on X, adding that the prime minister had become "toxic" not only within the Democratic Party but also among Republicans, some of whose leaders are now blaming him for their defeat.

On Wednesday, Trump acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, launched in February under pressure from Netanyahu, played a role in his party's defeat.

"If Israel wants to start rebuilding its very poor standing in the US, it must part ways with Netanyahu," Tibon said, adding that a failure to do so could lead "to very dangerous places".


  

  Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
    Read More »


The Democrats' landslide victory also raised concerns among right-wing Israeli politicians and commentators.

Journalist Ariel Kahana told Radio 103FM that "Israel suffered a very serious blow" on Tuesday's elections, as Israel "was on the ballot".

"Netanyahu is a burden on Israel," Kahana said.

Political analyst Kobby Barda of the Jewish People Policy Institute think tank said that Iran was the "big winner" of the US elections, while Netanyahu was the "huge loser".

"The face of Israel’s government can’t be Netanyahu anymore," right-winger Barda said, citing his unpopularity rates in the US.

Michael Oren, a former Israeli diplomat, warned that the triumphs of people like Sayed, who he called "a venomously anti-Israel candidate" and "antisemitic", could lead to catastrophic ramifications for Israel.

Oren warned that "the halt of military aid may be only the beginning", saying that intelligence and military systems sharing with the US, entry visas for Israelis and supplies of essential military components were all now at risk. He added that US sanctions against Israel were also a possibility.

"Thus, an era of half a century in US-Israel relations, as we have known it, comes to an end," Oren said, adding that "what lies ahead is clouded in uncertainty".

articles.title: Kirkland Lake Discoveries expands Mirado West gold zone beyond 1.1 kilometres
articles.description: Kirkland Lake Discoveries CEO Stefan Sklepowicz joined Steve Darling from Proactive to announce new diamond drilling results from four step-out holes at the Mirado West Zone, part of the company's KL South property in Kirkland Lake, Ontario. Sklepowicz told Proactive that the latest results have expanded the mineralized footprint of Mirado West to more than 1,100 metres of strike length, highlighting a system that hosts both high-grade gold veins and broad zones of bulk-tonnage mineralization. The drilling has intersected gold from less than 10 metres below surface to depths approaching 480 metres downhole, with the mineralized corridor remaining open in multiple directions. One of the standout results came from step-out hole KLM26-048, which intersected 10.53 grams per tonne gold over 9.20 metres, including a particularly high-grade interval of 31.93 g/t gold over 3.00 metres. The same hole also encountered a broad zone of bulk-tonnage mineralization at depth, returning 0.64 g/t gold over 68.00 metres, including a higher-grade section of 1.25 g/t gold over 26.50 metres. The company said the results demonstrate the potential for high-grade gold shoots to occur alongside wider, continuous zones of mineralization, providing opportunities to build both grade and potential resource volume. Additional step-out holes also returned repeated wide gold intervals, including zones measuring approximately 16 to 26 metres, supporting the company's interpretation that mineralization extends across a substantial corridor. Sklepowicz said the combination of high-grade intervals and broader mineralized zones is particularly encouraging, pointing to a system with the potential to host multiple styles of gold mineralization. Mirado West is located immediately adjacent to the Mirado South and Mirado North zones along the same structural trend. The expansion of Mirado West to more than 1.1 kilometres of strike length alongside Mirado South strengthens the company's view that these neighbouring zones could form part of a much larger, district-scale gold system. articles.title: Ameriwest advances Oregon copper-gold project with historic core resampling
articles.description: Ameriwest Critical Metals CEO David Watkinson joined Steve Darling from Proactive to discuss the company's efforts to advance the Bornite copper-gold-silver project in Oregon, including the reassessment of historic drill core, plans for an updated technical report and opportunities for additional exploration. Watkinson explained that the Bornite project was previously owned by Plexus Resources during the 1990s, when a pre-feasibility study and other technical work were completed. Ameriwest has since recovered a substantial portion of the historic drill core and transported it to Reno, Nevada, where the material is being logged and selected intervals resampled. The company has released results from the first three holes in a seven-hole resampling program. Watkins said the initial findings are generally consistent with historical results, with copper grades appearing somewhat higher and gold and silver values also showing improvements in several intervals. Additional assay results are expected as the remaining samples are processed, providing further information to compare against the original drilling data. The resampling initiative is designed to verify the historical exploration results and support the preparation of an updated technical report compliant with NI 43-101 standards. Ameriwest is targeting completion of that report in the first quarter of 2027. Alongside the technical work, the company is beginning the permitting process for additional confirmation drilling, which could take place next summer. A key focus is evaluating the potential of the project's breccia pipe deposit. Historical work identified a high-grade outer shell with grades exceeding 3% copper equivalent, while Ameriwest is also investigating whether the lower-grade interior portion of the structure could support economic mining under current metal price conditions. Watkinson said the company is undertaking technical studies to determine whether the interior of the breccia pipe could have mining potential, emphasizing that the work is intended to test that geological and economic concept. Ameriwest is also considering geophysical surveys to investigate whether additional breccia pipes may exist elsewhere in the area. The work could help identify extensions of the known mineralization at depth and investigate the possibility of a deeper feeder system. With historic core resampling underway, an updated technical report planned and permitting preparations beginning, Ameriwest is working to establish a clearer picture of the Bornite project's mineral potential and identify the next steps toward advancing the Oregon asset. #proactiveinvestors #ameriwestcriticalmetals #cse #awcm #otc #awlif #CopperExploration #GoldExploration #SilverExploration #BonnetProject #OregonMining #CriticalMetals #CopperMining #MineralExploration #MiningStocks #JuniorMining #NI43101

articles.description: Lightning Minerals Ltd managing director Troy Brice talked with Proactive about the completion of an expanded Phase 3 soil sampling program at the Warby Tungsten Project in North Queensland and the work now underway to refine targets for a maiden drill campaign. Brice said tungsten had emerged rapidly as an exploration focus at Warby after the company initially targeted gold at the project. articles.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
articles.description:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Abdallah al-Naami
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 13:47

        
      
    
      
    
                From children playing out to families queuing for food, indiscriminate Israeli shooting has made daily life a struggle for survival across Gaza
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Safia Abo Amra hold a photo of her granddaughter Fatima al-Bayouk, who was killed by Israeli gunfire earlier this month (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
                  Off
                  After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.

“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.
  
    



  



Despite everything she had endured, Bayouk had brought joy back into her grandmother’s life. Her uncle Ahmad Abo Amra remembered her as a bright, cheerful girl whose smile lifted the spirits of those around her.


'My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her'

- Safia Abo Amra, Palestinian grandmother 


“The best thing about Fatima was her smile that always brought joy to everyone around her. She was smart, responsible and loved happy occasions like weddings and family gatherings,” he said.

Her death reflects a wider pattern of indiscriminate Israeli gunfire that has become a daily threat to Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, particularly displaced families living near the so-called Yellow Line.

Israeli shooting from military positions, tanks and quadcopter drones has killed and wounded hundreds of civilians since the October 2025 ceasefire. It has also disrupted access to basic necessities and made everyday activities dangerous.

As Israel expands its control over more of the territory, families increasingly find themselves exposed to gunfire, with little protection and few places to seek safety.

A life cut short

For Bayouk’s family, her death was particularly devastating. She had already survived the loss of her immediate family in the early days of Israel’s genocide.

On 13 December 2023, an Israeli air strike targeted their home in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killing her family. Bayouk survived and went to live with her grandmother in Deir al-Balah, where Abo Amra and other relatives tried to rebuild her life amid the devastation of the war.


'With her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren'

- Safia  Abo Amro


“We did our best to provide everything Fatima needed and make her feel cared for and surrounded by people who love her,” Abo Amra said.

“I wanted to make up for the loss of her family, but with her beautiful soul, she was the one to help me through my grief for my daughter and grandchildren.”

Education remained an important part of Bayouk’s life as she grew up in her grandmother’s home. Concerned for her safety, Abo Amra refused to send her to a UN school after hearing that Israeli stray bullets frequently reached the area. Instead, she paid monthly fees to enrol her in a local school.

“I walked Fatima to school every day. She was very smart and always did her homework before playing,” Abo Amra said.

Her death reopened the grandmother’s wounds.

“I was shocked and couldn't speak or move. Her death was twice as painful for me; it reminded me of my daughter and grandchildren who were killed at the beginning of the war,” Abo Amra said. 

“My life was attached to Fatima’s. I wish I could die after her.”

  
  
      



    Fatima al-Bayouk liked to dress well, her family says (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  









Despite her young age, Bayouk left a lasting impression on those around her. She loved dressing up, particularly for family celebrations.

Her uncle Reda Abo Amra remembered how much she enjoyed choosing new clothes. The family had recently bought her winter clothes, but she never got the chance to wear them.

“She always liked to be well-dressed. We bought her new clothes for winter, but she was killed before she could wear them,” he told MEE.
  
    



  



Bayouk was not the first member of her family to be killed by Israeli gunfire. Six months before her death, her uncle Masoud Abo Amra, who was born with a mental disability, was shot in the neck while visiting his sister in Khan Younis.

“Masoud was Fatima's favourite uncle. She was devastated when she bid him farewell,” Ahmad said.

‘When the shooting starts, life stops’

For displaced families in Gaza, Israeli gunfire is not only a deadly threat but also a constant disruption to daily life.

Zaid al-Kafarna, 19, and his family of 10 were displaced from northern Gaza to the Um Duhair area, south of Deir al-Balah, days before the October 2025 ceasefire came into effect.

Kafarna said Israeli shooting was initially “occasional” and took place some distance from their tents. But it gradually became more frequent and moved closer to the camp. Over the past three months, he said, it had become a daily threat, frequently causing deaths, injuries and damage. 


  

  Gaza family mourns boys killed by Israel along Yellow Line
    Read More »


“I miraculously survived stray bullets several times. My friend and neighbour, Mohammad Aqel, was killed a few weeks ago by a stray bullet while he was preparing to return to northern Gaza,” Kafarna told MEE.

His mother, Shereen al-Kafarna, was recently wounded by an Israeli bullet while inside their tent. She described how the shooting brings life in the camp to a standstill.

“When the shooting starts, life stops in our camp. Neighbours warn each other. We leave everything and hold the children, then lie on the ground to avoid the bullets hitting around us. Everyone is terrified, especially the children,” she said.

The gunfire also disrupts Palestinians' efforts to secure basic necessities, including food and water.

“Sometimes while we are waiting in queues for water and food, Israeli tanks and quadcopter drones start shooting directly towards us,” Zaid said.

“Everyone panics. We lie on the ground at the side of the road, watching the aid trucks carrying our food and water drive away to escape the bullets. On those days, we don't have anything to eat or drink.” 

Nowhere to go

The pattern of daily Israeli shootings near the Yellow Line, alongside the ongoing expansion of Israel’s buffer zone in Gaza, raised questions among families about whether the gunfire is as random as it appears.

Many believe that the shootings appear to form part of a military tactic to force Palestinian families out of their homes and tents, allowing Israel to expand its control over more territory through force.
  
    



  



In the year following the ceasefire, Israeli control over Gaza grew from 53 to 70 percent, reflecting what the Palestinians describe as a systematic policy of territorial expansion.

Families living near the Yellow Line said the threat of stray bullets had forced several others to leave their camps.

“Watching families leave our camp every day makes us feel even more afraid. We wish we could move away from the bullets, but we have nowhere to go,” Shereen told MEE. 

“Even if we had somewhere to go, we can't afford the extremely expensive cost of transportation.”

With few options for escape, some families have resorted to building small sand barriers and digging trench-like holes inside and between their tents to shelter from the bullets.

  
  
      



    Shadi Siam dug a trench for his family next to their tent to take cover from Israeli gunfire (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
  











Next to his tent, Shadi Siam dug a small trench to protect his family of five.

“I fear for my children's lives every time I hear Israeli stray bullets flying low,” Siam told MEE.

“My children wake up terrified, and I carry them to the hole where we all hide for two to five hours until the shooting stops,” he added.

“I don't know how I will protect them when the winter comes, and the hole becomes unusable.”

                  Gaza City, occupied Palestine

articles.title: ‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
articles.description:
‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE correspondent
 on 
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 09:10

        
      
    
      
    
                Renewed fighting around Taiz has left children with nightmares, bedwetting and constant fear, while schools remain closed and psychological support is scarce
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A woman sits with two children in a classroom converted into a temporary shelter for displaced people at Sawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
                  Off
                  In October, as clashes reached Taghreed Abdulellah’s area, located about 30km from Yemen's Taiz city, the mother of three found herself unable to flee with her children, as battles had already broken out in their village.

She had no choice but to gather her children, aged four, seven and 10, in the hallway to protect them from potential blasts or shrapnel coming through the windows.

“Their father wasn’t at home; it was just them and me. The clashes were outside, and an explosion went off right near our home, leaving the children terrified and crying for hours,” Abdulellah told Middle East Eye. 

“I couldn’t stop them from crying; in fact, I broke down and joined them at times.”

When the fighting quieted down, the children would stop crying, and some neighbours visited to boost their morale.
  
    



  



However, as soon as the battles flared up again, the crying resumed.

“This continued for four days until the fierce battles moved away from our area. But my children’s lives have completely changed for the worse,” she explained.

“My children are always angry, and the two younger ones are now suffering from bedwetting, while the eldest constantly talks about losing his life and believes he will be killed at any moment, rather than thinking about his studies and future as he used to.” 

Abdulellah’s children used to sleep in their own room, but since the fighting started, they do not dare to sleep alone. The whole family now sleeps in one room, with the two younger children sleeping in their mother’s arms.

“Nightmares terrify them every night, and during the day they refuse to leave the house because they feel they will be killed or injured if they go outside. So, they spend the entire day indoors,” Abdulellah said.

Battles in Taiz    

Public schools across Taiz governorate, including Taiz city and rural areas, have been closed since 4 October, as it is unsafe for children to attend school.

It is also unsafe for children to play outside, as shelling and air strikes hit almost every district in the area. 
  
    



  



Abdulellah believes it is unsafe for her children to go outside, yet she wants them to be able to so they can resume a normal life and heal from the psychological trauma they are facing.


  

  Yemen war: Taiz villagers face tough choices as fighters move in
    Read More »


“It is the first time in my life that I have seen my children feel so lost. They don’t want to play, they don’t want to study, and they only talk about the war. I am worried this will impact the rest of their lives even when normal life returns.”

On 4 October, Houthi forces advanced into large areas of Taiz governorate, taking control of most of the governorate and seizing all roads leading to Taiz city.

Battles are currently ongoing around Taiz city and in rural areas, as the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, attempt to push from Taiz toward Lahij governorate while also trying to take full control of Taiz city.

Saudi-led air strikes have targeted Houthi forces in the rural areas of Taiz and around Taiz city, which have also taken a heavy toll on children in those areas.

The World Health Organization has reported that 1,677 people were killed and more than 7,395 injured across Yemen between August and late October 2026 amid renewed clashes between government forces and Houthis.

The executive manager of the Taiz Human Rights Centre civil society organization, Mazen Aqlan, told MEE that 19 children were killed and 49 injured in Taiz governorate in October 2026. 

Severe psychological impact   

Odai, 13, is a child in Taiz city whose life has also completely changed. He used to spend his mornings at school and his afternoons playing with friends. But since 4 October, he has spent most of his days and nights scrolling through his phone, only leaving the house briefly to sit with friends and adults under a nearby tree.

The main issue, however, lies in the photos and videos he views on his mobile, along with the stories he hears from adults about what happened in 2015 when fighting reached their neighbourhood and civilians, including children, were killed or injured. 

“Life isn’t easy, and death is close to everyone,” Odai told MEE. “We were focused on our studies and weren’t aware that a person could lose their life in a single minute. That is what happened to many people, both nowadays and during the last war.”


  

  'If Houthi shelling does not kill us, the diseases will': Yemenis in besieged Taiz bemoan neglect
    Read More »


Odai, who is in the seventh grade, appears mature for his age, but the ongoing developments and the stories he hears have shifted his priorities from his education to thoughts of the afterlife, something that is not typical for a child his age.

When asked about his priorities and whether they should focus on his studies, he laughed and said: “Studying is important, but there is no guarantee we will stay alive until schools reopen. Death is closer to us than resuming our education.”

MEE spoke with Odai’s father, in his 50s, who preferred to remain anonymous. He confirmed that Odai was not like this until last month, when he heard a story about a child killed in the city and saw related photos and videos, leaving him deeply affected.

“We do our best to keep our children away from the fighting. We keep them at home and don’t allow them to venture outside, especially to far areas, but it is difficult to keep a child mentally stable in this environment,” Odai’s father told MEE.

“Mobile phones and the stories they hear from friends leave a severe psychological impact on children, especially when they see photos of killed children. That is out of our control.”

He added that such horrifying scenes impact even adults like himself, not just children. He believes the best solution is for local authorities and organisations to provide immediate psychological support during these difficult times.

“During wartime, everyone worries about the physical safety of their children, and only a few care about their psychological well-being - which is just as important, as its long-term impact can be devastating,” he said.

Gap between needs and support

The Taiz Human Rights Centre's Aqlan told MEE: “There are more than 100,000 children in Taiz governorate who have witnessed the horrors of war and been traumatised by its shells, explosions and tragedies. They are in urgent need of psychological care.”

He identified the group most in need of psychological support as the families who have lost loved ones, had their homes shelled, been displaced or have directly suffered from the consequences of the war. 

  
  
      



    Women and children gather at a temporary shelter for displaced people at Shawkani school, north of Aden, Yemen, 15 September 2026 (AFP)
  




  
    



  









In mid-September, prior to the recent escalation around Taiz city, the UN children's agency Unicef reported that over 57,000 children had been displaced in just a two-week period.

While the Taiz Human Rights Centre estimates that over 100,000 children need psychological support in the governorate, the UN reported earlier this year, before the recent military escalation, that 12.2 million children across the country were in need of humanitarian assistance.

The Social Affairs and Labour Office in Taiz governorate stated on Sunday that non-governmental humanitarian organisations operating in the governorate provided psychosocial support services to 719 children, while 219 boys and girls received psychological first aid sessions.

Future at risk  

Psychologist Saba al-Sabri, who works with several institutions providing psychological support in Taiz, confirmed that clear behavioural changes in children have been observed over the past month.

“These behaviours include non-acceptance of others, grief over loss, continuous fear, nervousness, bedwetting, clinging to parents even during sleep, and a total loss of motivation to learn because they believe they will die or become disabled, all of which severely affect the children’s future,” Sabri told MEE. 


  

  Yemen: Parents in Taiz demand answers over alleged rape of their children
    Read More »


She said that the counselling sessions provided by humanitarian initiatives and organisations remain far too few compared to the immense need that has persisted for over 11 years.

“These recent events have added new children to the list of those in need, making psychological support vital to preserving the next generation.”

Sabri pointed out that some parents do not realise the severity of psychological trauma on children, and instead focus solely on basic survival, which represents a disaster for the child.

“Ignoring a child’s feelings and failing to sit and communicate with them leaves a deep negative impact on their well-being.”

Most children currently do not leave their homes. Sabri noted that children are naturally energetic and need to play outside; depriving them of this heightens stress and nervousness, weakens their personality development and worsens their mood.

Abdulellah, the mother of the three children who witnessed the fighting and were traumatised, strongly believes in psychological treatment, but it remains inaccessible to them.

“If psychological treatment were available, I wouldn’t hesitate to take my children. But we are in a time of war, and it is hard to access such services since they are usually only available in the city.”

articles.title: 'Show courage' and end Netanyahu's government, Tibi urges Israeli opposition leader
articles.description:
'Show courage' and end Netanyahu's government, Tibi urges Israeli opposition leader

    
    

        
    
                Speaking to David Hearst, Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi urged Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to show political courage and work with Arab parties to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rule.

"I hope Eisenkot will be courageous enough to go forward and form a minority government, which will end this government of Netanyahu immediately," Tibi said.

In the latest episode of the David Hearst Podcast, Ahmad Tibi, founder and leader of the Ta’al party, said there was no democratic justification for ruling out cooperation with Palestinian representatives in the Knesset this time around.    

Tibi’s party is part of the Joint List, alongside two other Palestinian-led parties, Hadash and Balad. Together, they won 11 seats. Another Palestinian party, Ra’am, secured eight, giving the two slates a combined 19 seats - a record for Palestinian parties in parliament.  

The results mean that neither a Netanyahu-led nor an Eisenkot-led bloc can secure a 61-seat majority without Palestinian parties.


Speaking to David Hearst, Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi urged Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to show political courage and work with Arab parties to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rule. https://t.co/EPe8QRL6v7

articles.title: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
articles.description:
Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

    
    

        
    
                After finishing her homework, Fatima al-Bayouk went to play with her cousins outside her grandmother’s home in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, when an Israeli bullet struck her neck.

Moments later, the eight-year-old Palestinian girl returned home trembling, blood soaking her shirt. She screamed that her cousin had been shot, unaware that she had been hit herself.

The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries.

For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life.

“Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. I have seven sons and six daughters, yet Fatima was more precious to me than all of them,” Abo Amra told Middle East Eye.

Read more: Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families

articles.title: Israeli forces kill 19 Palestinians in three days of Gaza attacks
articles.description:
Israeli forces kill 19 Palestinians in three days of Gaza attacks

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:29

        
      
    
      
    
                Latest attacks include air strikes on a university and police and security personnel in Khan Younis
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Palestinians inspect the site of an Israeli strike after a vehicle was hit in Gaza City, 2 November 2026 (Reuters/Dawoud Abu Alkas)
                  Off
                  Israeli forces have killed 19 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip since Saturday, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

The ministry said on Tuesday afternoon that six people had been killed in the previous 24 hours, following 13 deaths over the weekend.

One Palestinian succumbed to his wounds on Tuesday morning after Israeli forces bombed the displacement camp where he was staying in Khan Younis.

Another was killed in an air strike targeting a group of people at the University College of Applied Sciences (UCAS) in Khan Younis.

Israeli attacks on school pupils and university students across the Gaza Strip have increased in recent weeks, following the start of the new academic year.
  
    



  



At least 14 pupils and four teachers were killed in Gaza in October, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education.

Three employees of the Islamic University were also killed in an Israeli bombing on campus last month.

The ministry further reported that more than 97 percent of schools and universities in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed by Israeli attacks.

The remaining educational institutions and alternative learning facilities continue to face the threat of further attacks and damage, it added. 

Elsewhere, Gaza's Ministry of Interior reported an Israeli air strike targeting police officers and security personnel in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis.

Several people were killed and wounded, the ministry said, without providing a final death toll. 

Violations of ceasefire

The attacks come as Israel continues to violate the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza.
  
    



  



The US-mediated agreement was intended to halt Israel's genocide by ending the bombardment and lifting restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid.


  

  Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
    Read More »


However, Israel has continued to carry out near-daily air strikes and demolitions of homes.

According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, Israeli forces have killed nearly 1,600 Palestinians since the ceasefire came into effect, including more than 340 children.

A further 5,700 people have been wounded.

The overall Palestinian death toll since the genocide began in October 2023 has reached at least 74,600, according to the ministry. Thousands more people remain missing or buried under the rubble.

Israeli authorities have also continued to impose tight restrictions on the entry of aid and goods into Gaza.

An average of just 200 trucks have been allowed into the territory each day, well below the agreed 600 and the estimated minimum required to meet Gaza's needs.

According to Gaza's Government Media Office, Israeli forces have committed 5,989 violations of the ceasefire since it took effect on 11 October 2025.

These include air strikes, shootings, home demolitions, raids and arbitrary arrests.

articles.title: Israel’s election shows its democracy is a sham, but the West can’t stop buying the lie
How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
articles.description:
How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Lubna Masarwa
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 14:39

        
      
    
      
    
                In Israel today, it doesn't really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Right-wing demonstrators gather in support of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who failed to secure a majority in Israeli elections, in Tel Aviv on 31 October 2026 (Jack Guez/AFP)
                  Off
                  A day before the Israeli elections, I was walking through a well-heeled, leafy neighbourhood in West Jerusalem, five minutes from President Issac Herzog’s official residence.

I was on my way to interview an expert on Palestinian citizens of Israel, who were expected to vote in large numbers for the first time.

Three children - they could not have been more than seven or eight - jumped off the slides in a playground and ran towards me. 

One of them asked whom I was going to vote for. A funny question, I thought, coming from kids.  

I told them I would vote for the Joint List. The leader of the group asked, “What is the Joint List? Is it Bibi?” I said no, without explaining that it was an Arab bloc of parties. 
  
    



  



The kid said: “So you’re not voting for Netanyahu?”

I said no. He spat at me, and the other two gave me the middle finger. 

They must have thought I was a Jew defecting from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp. I wondered what they would have done if they knew I was Palestinian.

Kids spitting at a middle-aged woman didn’t seem to bother any of the passersby.

To liberal Zionists, this election was a debate about the boundaries of Israeli democracy, and whether it could include us as Arabs.


Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians


But the more I think about it, something far deeper is going on than mere hatred of a minority group, deeply entrenched though that is. The reaction to 7 October merely brought it out into the open.

Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians, and calling openly for more occupation, expulsion and deportation.

Palestinians who live in the city have to hold their breath if they want to live with this reality. They have no right to complain against another sticker calling on them to be killed or expelled.

It’s not just in every debate in this election campaign. You can hear it in small conversations in the street: “We will not sit with the Arabs.”

All the discussion is about how to build coalitions without the votes of the Arabs. 

Palestinians vote for survival

Three Israeli political parties ran on platforms that openly support the deportation, displacement and expulsion of Palestinians - even those with Israeli citizenship.

Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and head of the Religious Zionism party, has made “Judaising” the Galilee and Negev regions of Israel, where many Palestinians citizens live, a key feature of his election campaign.

All of this was orchestrated by the person who by rights should be Israel’s outgoing prime minister, Netanyahu, but who continues as its caretaker.
  
    



  



Haaretz analysed Netanyahu’s social media activity on election day. Every second post by the prime minister was against Arabs, laying the groundwork for claims about the integrity of the vote.



The response of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up a fifth of the population, was immediate. They flocked to the polls, gaining an unheard-of 19 seats, and became the third-largest parliamentary bloc after Likud and Yashar.

Those who had boycotted elections for their entire lives went to vote for the first time.

This was not some sudden revelation. Every Palestinian understood that they were only part of Israel as window dressing, to make it look democratic, but with no meaningful ability to change their lives. In the past, just over half of them voted.


The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself


But this time, it was different.

The Palestinians of Israel know that what happened in Gaza, and is continuing to happen in the occupied West Bank, could happen to them too.

Israel committed genocide and got away with it. This vote is a survival vote; an expressed, very existential fear. 

Palestinian sociologist Ameer Fakhoury told Middle East Eye: “The moment your existence becomes the central concern, the very meaning of citizenship changes. A citizen, in the substantive sense, should not have to engage in politics simply to avoid death.

“This is not how citizenship is supposed to function. When survival becomes the dominant motivation, the boundaries of ordinary political participation collapse. The symbolic and substantive meaning of citizenship is fundamentally undermined.”

Such a result in a “normal” democratic country would have ended with the opposition winning.

But not in Israel. Netanyahu’s initial loss became an orgy, a festival of racism against Palestinians.

No good or bad Arabs

Channel 12 News reported that on election day and its aftermath, there was a 400 percent rise in racist discourse against Arabs on social media, as Arabs were accused of stealing the elections.

Ayala Hasson, the veteran journalist of Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan 11, claimed, without any proof, that some of the 19 newly elected Knesset members from the Palestinian-led parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, “transferred money to Hamas”.

Hasson, a pro-Netanyahu journalist, also questioned the integrity of the elections, saying that Palestinian voters received envelopes with money as part of an illegal voter mobilisation campaign.

It doesn’t really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt.


  

  I have boycotted Israeli elections for years, but this time I will vote
    Read More »


Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has openly adopted a Zionist agenda by acknowledging the Jewish state and calling for national service.

He received the same treatment. This means that even Palestinians who strip themselves of their national identity cannot be part of a political system designed for Jews only.

The same thing happened to Lucy Aharish, an Arab journalist married to an Israeli Jew who served as a combat soldier in the reserves during the genocide in Gaza.

Aharish was savaged by prominent figures in Likud.

Itzik Bonzel, a Likud candidate, posted on Facebook: “You can walk around our streets as much as you like, but merely living among us does not make you Israeli in any way, and you will never be part of us, nor part of the people of Israel.”

Aharish is an opponent of the Palestinian national cause. Bonzel said she was “a foreign body, without any real roots in this land, and you will never be an Israeli”, concluding with a threat: “Know your place.”

Arabs in Israel can no longer ignore the fact that for large groups in Israel, possibly now the majority, there are no good or bad Arabs. It matters not who goes over to their side.
  
    



  



For them, Palestinians are illegitimate and should be expelled from the Jewish state.

The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself - and this should not be ignored by the Palestinian leadership.

I was asked in an interview with a Canadian radio station whether I thought Palestinians would vote again in future elections. Did this result inspire them?

For a moment I was taken aback by the stupidity of this question.

“I am not inspired, I am terrified,” I replied.
