articles.title: Israeli prison guards ‘shot prominent Palestinian detainees nine times’
articles.description:
Israeli prison guards ‘shot prominent Palestinian detainees nine times’

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 15:09

        
      
    
      
    
                Hassan Salameh was beaten and shot inside his cell, possibly with rubber-coated bullets, after Ben-Gvir stormed the prison, his fiancee and a prisoner rights group say
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A Palestinian boy holds a framed image of Hassan Salameh during a protest against the Israeli death penalty law for Palestinians in Gaza City 31 March (Reuters/Dawoud Abu Alkas)
                  Off
                  Israeli prison guards shot and wounded prominent Palestinian detainee Hassan Salameh nine times last month, his fiancee and a prisoners' rights group have said.

The assault on Salameh, 55, came after National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir stormed his cell and filmed himself threatening to kill him.

The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society (PPS), which monitors the conditions of Palestinian detainees, said it received information about the assault following a visit to Salameh by a lawyer on Monday.

Information provided to the group and Salameh’s fiancee, Ghufran Zamel, indicated that he had been severely beaten and shot nine times.

The type of ammunition used and the precise circumstances of the shooting remain unclear.
  
    



  



Israeli prison guards have recently stepped up the use of rubber-coated bullets against prisoners, firing at them from close range inside their cells.

The practice has caused severe injuries and potentially irreversible harm, according to rights groups. 

PPS said Israeli restrictions on prison visits had prevented the lawyer from obtaining further details.

“This has raised serious concerns about the prisoner's fate and underscores the urgent need to disclose the circumstances of the incident and guarantee his physical safety,” the group said.



Zamel told local media that Salameh was beaten before Ben Gvir's visit and after he left. An Israeli force stormed the cell, subjecting him to a severe beating, including blows to the face, before firing nine bullets at him.

Three days after the assault, Salameh was taken to have his injuries photographed. He was then returned to his cell without medical treatment and given only painkillers, despite the injuries he had sustained, Zamel said.

According to Zamel, Monday's visit by the lawyer confirmed that Salameh was still suffering from the effects of the assault and remained in poor health. He appeared visibly exhausted.

PPS said the attack came amid what it described as a campaign targeting prominent Palestinian prisoners, which goes “beyond repression and punishment” and places their lives at risk.

“Prisoner leaders are facing various forms of physical and psychological torture, systematic crackdowns and public threats to kill them made by Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir,” the group said.

“The continuation of these policies, alongside restrictions on visits and the absence of independent oversight, paves the way for further violations and deprives prisoners of even the most basic protection.”

Escalating abuse 

Born in the Khan Younis refugee camp in southern Gaza in 1971, Salameh became involved in Palestinian resistance against the Israeli occupation after the outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987.

He later became a leading figure in the armed wing of Hamas, the al-Qassam Brigades. In 1996, Israel convicted him of orchestrating several bombings that killed and wounded scores of Israelis.
  
    



  



Salameh said the attacks were carried out in response to Israel's assassination of Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash earlier that year. 


  

  Israeli guards ‘crushed’ Palestinian prisoner’s testicle with rubber bullet
    Read More »


He was sentenced to 48 life terms and has spent a total of 14 years in solitary confinement since his imprisonment 30 years ago.

In September, Ben Gvir posted a video showing himself in Salameh’s cell, surrounded by security guards, as he told him that he wanted to "execute" him.

The minister also vowed to ensure prisoners such as Salameh were "put to death" if he became defence minister.

Palestinian prisoners, particularly prominent figures such as Salameh, have long faced abuse by Israeli prison authorities.

However, reports of abuse have escalated since the Gaza war and genocide began in October 2023. Several rights groups have accused Israeli prison authorities of widespread torture, physical assaults, sexual violence, starvation, medical neglect and humiliation of prisoners since then. 

Last month, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel said they had collected 21 testimonies documenting what they described as a “dangerous practice” of prison guards firing rubber-coated bullets at prisoners from close range.

In one incident, an Israeli prison guard seriously wounded a Palestinian prisoner by firing rubber-coated bullets at his testicle. His right testicle was “completely crushed” and had to be surgically removed.

articles.title: Israeli ex-generals condemn settler violence, help Palestinian farmers
articles.description:
Israeli ex-generals condemn settler violence, help Palestinian farmers

    
    

        
    
                A group of senior Israeli ex-military officials helped Palestinian farmers on Tuesday to harvest olives, in a gesture of solidarity amid an upsurge in extremist settler violence targeting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

"When I see what is going on here, when I see these guys come... and hit women and kids, it reminds me of stories from my parents from the time when the Jewish people suffered," said former Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, who compared the settler attacks to pogroms.

Ben-Reuven said he began organising a group of around 30 senior military officials - including six generals - several months ago, following an increase in settler violence that many Palestinians say is enabled by the Israeli military.

"Occupation is the main problem of Israeli society. I believe we must deal with it. We cannot ignore it. We must try to solve it together with the Palestinians," said former Colonel Doron Meinert.

Reporting by Reuters

articles.title: Opposition leader Lapid accuses Netanyahu backers of attempts at 'crushing' Israel's democracy
articles.description:
Opposition leader Lapid accuses Netanyahu backers of attempts at 'crushing' Israel's democracy

    
    

        
    
                Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused supporters of Benajmin Netanyahu's government of attempting to "crush" Tel Aviv's democracy.

"What we are seeing tonight is an attempt to crush democracy and steal the election with the help of government plants in the security system," he said in a post on X.

"This is a direct threat to our democracy from people who are unwilling to admit defeat," Lapid added.

The Israeli opposition leaders also called on state institution to "stand firm" against the move, calling on his counterparts to "put everything aside and form a government as quickly as possible".

Lapid's remarks come amid reports of Shin Bet chief David Zini seeking to question three Palestinian party leaders in an investigation into possible foreign interference in the election.

Netanyahu’s camp has been repeatedly accused in recent days of seeking to delegitimise the election results after claims that the vote for Palestinian-led parties, who won a historic 19 seats out of 120, were manipulated by foreign interference.

Law enforcement officials have found no evidence of such claims or a justification to question the leaders.

The mass participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s election last week obstructed both Netanyahu and his challenger Gadi Eisenkott from gaining the 61 seats required to secure a parliamentary majority and form a government.

articles.title: Iran’s Khamenei says US hostility will persist regardless of party in power
Iran’s Khamenei says US election results will not end hostility towards Tehran
articles.description:
Iran’s Khamenei says US election results will not end hostility towards Tehran

    
    

        
    
                Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei says Washington will continue its confrontation with Tehran despite the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories.

In a message carried by state news agency IRNA, he rejected suggestions that “factional shifts” would “dissuade it from its hostility towards the Iranian nation”.

He said Washington seeks the “unconditional surrender of the Iranian nation”.

Referring to the US-Israeli war on Iran, Khamenei said the US had “suffered an irreversible decline” after a “self-made scandal”, adding that “the process of its collapse has accelerated”.

articles.title: Iran defence spokesperson says US vote exposes failure of Trump’s war policies
articles.description:
Iran defence spokesperson says US vote exposes failure of Trump’s war policies

    
    

        
    
                Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesperson General Reza Talaeinik has portrayed the US midterm election results as further evidence that Trump and Netanyahu’s policies have failed.

Writing on social media, he called it an opportunity to “revisit the crimes of global arrogance, especially America, and to renew our pledge to resist interventionism”.

“Today, with the failure of Trump and Netanyahu’s warmongering policies becoming more apparent and the trend of their hegemony’s collapse in the world, the steadfastness of the Iranian nation is more than ever inspiring to free nations,” he wrote.

His comments follow a warning from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei that Tehran cannot trust Washington and that changes in US political leadership will not end its hostility towards Iran.

Israeli settlers seize eight homes in occupied West Bank village west of Jericho

Palestinian security sources told Wafa that the settlers, accompanied by their families, stormed the eight homes, which were empty at the time of the raid, and smashed their doors, remaining inside the property.

Israeli forces also stormed Jericho and its refugee camps on Wednesday evening, deploying military vehicles along the city’s streets, according to Wafa.

They also reported that Israeli soldiers raided the area surrounding the Thabet Thabet Governmental Hospital in Tulkarm, in the occupied West Bank, and ransacked the home of Mohammed Ibrahim Shahada, secretary of Fatah in Tulkarm refugee camp on Wednesday.

articles.title: Dapo Akande elected as ICJ judge, restoring British presence inside highest UN court
articles.description:
Dapo Akande elected as ICJ judge, restoring British presence inside highest UN court

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Sondos Asem
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:19

        
      
    
      
    
                Oxford professor argued against annexation of Palestinian territory and challenged Britain’s legal positions on Chagos, Iraq and Syria
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Dapo Akande addresses the International Court of Justice on behalf of Japan during hearings on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory, in The Hague on 22 February, 2024 (UN Photo/ICJ-CIJ/Frank van Beek)
                  Off
                  British international lawyer Dapo Akande has been elected to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), restoring a British presence on the United Nations’ highest court after almost a decade.

Akande was elected judge on Tuesday alongside France’s Francois Alabrune, Singapore’s Rena Lee, Jordan’s Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud and Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa. Nine candidates contested the five seats. 

Their nine-year terms begin on 6 February 2027. Hmoud and Okowa, already serving after elections to fill vacancies, secured full terms.

As a lawyer and scholar, Akande has helped advance arguments on proving genocide and the illegality of annexing Palestinian territory, and he is expected to sit on the bench as the court decides on the ongoing case brought by South Africa accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in Gaza.

Akande, Oxford’s Chichele Professor of Public International Law and a member of the UN International Law Commission, will become the first British judge on the court since 2018.
  
    



  



The British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband welcomed the election as "a victory for the UK’s commitment to the rule of law and our ability to stand up for our values on the world stage".

Akande describes himself as a “generalist public international lawyer”, whose work spans armed conflict, international criminal law, human rights, international organisations and the settlement of disputes between states.

“Dapo is a careful, nuanced jurist and a precise and effective communicator,” said Janina Dill, Akande’s co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law, and Armed Conflict.

“As a colleague I have most admired his even keel and wisdom. I am glad the court can benefit from these qualities at this moment in time," she told Middle East Eye after Akande's election.

Candidates needed an absolute majority in separate votes in the General Assembly and Security Council, 97 votes and eight votes respectively. The council’s permanent members have no veto in judicial elections.

The court’s judges serve independently of their governments. 

Based in The Hague, the ICJ settles disputes between states and issues authoritative advisory opinions. Unlike the International Criminal Court (ICC), it determines state responsibility and does not prosecute individuals.
  
    



  



Its judgments in disputes are binding on the parties, although enforcement can depend on action by states and a politically divided Security Council.

Previous ICJ interventions

Akande’s election comes as the ICJ prepares to issue a judgment in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar over atrocities against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority. Akande served as counsel for Britain in this case as part of the UK’s legal team alongside Alison Macdonald KC and Naomi Hart.


  

  The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
    Read More »


In this case, Britain intervened jointly with Canada, Denmark, France, Germany and the Netherlands to present arguments about interpreting the Genocide Convention.

Their submissions warned against making proof of genocidal intent so demanding that findings become practically impossible.

The states also argued that genocide encompasses acts beyond killing, including sexual violence and the imposition of destructive living conditions. Children’s particular vulnerabilities must inform assessments of serious harm, deprivation and displacement, they added.

The Myanmar case, in which judgment is scheduled for 19 November, has become a focus of US attacks on the court.

Last month, US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused the Gambia's ad hoc judge, who is the latest Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay of seeking to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against American and allied soldiers.


'If elected, I will decide cases on the basis of a faithful and impartial application of the law'

- Dapo Akande, newly elected ICJ judge


Waltz warned that Washington would be “watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely”, invoking US sanctions against the ICC.

Akande has also addressed the ICJ on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory, appearing for Japan during the court’s advisory opinion proceedings on the illegality of Israel’s occupation. 

Akande argued that a state could not get around the ban on taking land by force simply by never formally announcing it had annexed it.

He told the judges that moving populations, seizing land, evicting residents, building long-term infrastructure and exploiting natural resources such as water could amount to annexation in practice, especially when officials described those changes as permanent.

He also argued that a state could not keep territory it had seized by claiming self-defence. Self-defence allowed a country to protect land it already had, not to gain more, he said, adding: “Permanent annexation can never be a proportionate response to an armed attack.”

Criticism of UK positions

Despite British support for his candidacy, Akande has previously challenged London’s positions before the court.

In the 2018 hearings on the Chagos Islands, which Britain separated from Mauritius before the Indian Ocean island became independent, he appeared for Zambia to rebut the UK's arguments.

Britain had argued that the matter was a territorial dispute between it and Mauritius, and that the court should not rule on it without British consent. Akande rejected that, telling the judges: “This case is about the international law obligations regarding decolonisation.”


  

  Who is Phoebe Okowa? The newly elected ICJ judge and her opinions on Israel-Palestine
    Read More »


He argued that the right of colonised peoples to decide their own future, known under international law as self-determination, concerned all countries, not just the two involved.

He also challenged Britain’s argument that this right was not yet part of international law in 1965, when Chagos was separated from Mauritius.

To make the point, he cited Britain’s own statements from that period accepting that all peoples had that right.

His criticism of British legal arguments has also extended to military action in the Middle East.

In an April 2018 opinion commissioned by then Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, Akande rejected the government’s justification for air strikes against Syria's Assad government.

Akande described its position as “significantly flawed”, concluding: “The military action taken was not in accordance with the United Nations Charter and international law.”

He argued that international law did not recognise the unilateral right of humanitarian intervention claimed by Britain. Even if such a right existed, he said, the strikes did not appear to meet the government’s own conditions.

Akande has also argued against the UK's participation in the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

In 2010, he led a group of academics in a submission to the Iraq Inquiry challenging the legal case for the invasion.
  
    



  



The government had argued that the Security Council’s 1990 authorisation to use force against Iraq, after it invaded Kuwait, could be revived more than a decade later because Iraq had breached the terms of the 1991 ceasefire. The submission called this “an untenable interpretation of the UN Charter”.

The submission also argued that even if the argument held, the UN Security Council’s resolution of November 2002 did not meet its conditions, so the attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, had been wrong to conclude the invasion was lawful.

In his statement as an ICJ candidate, Akande emphasised legal rigour, cooperation across legal traditions and judicial independence.

"If elected, I will decide cases on the basis of a faithful and impartial application of the law having listened carefully to the arguments of participants in the proceedings," he wrote.

articles.title: UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools
articles.description:
UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Oscar Rickett
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:30

        
      
    
      
    
                The Good Law Project and British Jewish group Na'amod tell MEE contested IHRA definition protects Israel, not Jewish students
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Police officers intervene as a pro-Israel banner is held during a rally in London on 16 November 2024 (AFP)
                  Off
                  The British government is being challenged legally over its recommendation for schools to adopt the contested IHRA definition of antisemitism.

The Good Law Project launched a legal challenge against the government on Monday. The group’s executive director Jo Maugham told Middle East Eye he was worried that “rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism… could be among the drivers of antisemitism”. 

“Antisemitism and the rise of antisemitism in Britain and around the world are very real things, and I want to say to British Jews who are at the sharp end, I hear your pain,” Maugham said.

“But I also worry - and it's a point I've made many times - that rules which conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and that unjustifiably constrain the freedom properly and vigorously to criticise Israel, could be amongst the drivers of antisemitism.”

The UK Department of Education’s move to encourage schools to adopt the IHRA definition follows the recommendation made in British education official and academic David Bell's recently published report on antisemitism in the country's schools and colleges.
  
    



  



The Bell report has been questioned for misrepresenting its findings, equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, and surveying small numbers of students from a narrow age bracket.

The controversy surrounding the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, which was originally formulated in 2004 as a non-legally binding tool to assist in monitoring antisemitism, comes mainly from the fact that seven of its 11 “illustrations” of antisemitism include references to Israel.


'Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job'

- Na'amod


The definition’s lead author, Kenneth Stern, has warned against its use as a disciplinary or legal instrument, arguing that it may risk restricting legitimate political expression.

In 2018, leading human rights lawyer Geoffrey Robertson issued a legal opinion stating that the definition is “likely in practice to chill free speech” by encouraging complaints against legitimate criticism of Israel.

The British Jewish group Na’amod, which also opposes the imposition of the IHRA definition, told MEE: “Jewish pupils should be safe at school, and antisemitism has to be taken seriously. The IHRA definition doesn’t do that job.”

“Its examples run criticism of Israel together with hatred of Jews, and in universities it has overwhelmingly been used to censor speech about Israel rather than to protect Jews,” a spokesperson for the group added.

“In schools, that leaves teachers policing children who talk about Gaza or the Nakba, instead of tackling real anti-Jewish racism. It also fails Jewish pupils, many of whom don’t tie their Jewishness to support for the Israeli state.”

The Bell review

The IHRA definition has been formally adopted by 47 countries.

Its adoption in British schools was one of 27 recommendations made in the Bell review. Following its publication on 21 October, it was widely reported that “three in five” Jewish students had experienced antisemitism in English schools.

This figure came from a survey of 5,000 students, 92 of whom were Jews aged, between 16 and 18. Seventy of those students responded to a question about whether they had personally experienced or witnessed antisemitism, with 29 of them - 41 percent, or around “two in five” rather than “three in five” - saying they had.


  

  UK antisemitism report found increase in 'anti-Israel' sentiment, not 'anti-Jewish' attitudes
    Read More »


The Bell review itself acknowledged that this was a “low sample size” and should be “treated with caution”. It also found that “anti-Jewish attitudes are typically less prevalent and have remained more stable, whereas anti-Israel sentiments are more prevalent and have been increasing”.

Middle East Eye asked the UK Department for Education about its plans to adopt the IHRA definition and about whether it had considered the warnings - including from the definition’s lead author - about the “chilling effect” the definition can have on pro-Palestinian expression and criticism of Israel.

“Antisemitism is a growing problem across society, including in our schools and colleges, and Jewish children and staff should never face hatred or prejudice in education,” a Department for Education spokesperson said in response.

“That is why we have accepted all 27 of Sir David Bell’s recommendations and are acting on them, including encouraging schools and colleges to adopt the IHRA working definition of antisemitism.

“The IHRA definition has been adopted by 47 countries and countless public bodies and can provide a practical framework for teachers and pupils, and help give greater clarity on how to identify and tackle antisemitism wherever it occurs.”

'Consistency is what we want'

Bell’s review recommends separate measures for tackling anti-Jewish hatred, distinct from existing anti-racism and anti-bullying policies. The National Education Union has criticised the move, warning it risks “creating a hierarchy of racism”.

The Good Law Project and Na’amod both told MEE that the British government should be consistent in how it deals with racism and not apply special treatment to antisemitism.


'It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions. We think it is necessary in a moral society'

- Jo Maugham, Good Law Project


“What we really want is for government to be consistent in how it tackles hate speech,” Maugham said. 

“The rules that apply to one minoritised group should also be the rules that are applied to other minoritised groups… Consistency is what we want.”

“Antisemitism should not be taught as exceptional,” the spokesperson for Na’amod said. “It should be taught alongside racism and Islamophobia, because these struggles are bound together and the people who fight one are the natural allies of those who fight the others.

“Treating antisemitism as a special case with its own rulebook prevents that learning and sets Jewish safety apart from everyone else’s.”

Gary Spedding, a cross-party political consultant on Israel-Palestine, told MEE he thought Bell’s review was “sloppy, misleading and inaccurate”, and that it was part of a “systemic, legal and institutional dismantling of any support for Palestine, or any education and discussion about Palestinian history and existence within the UK education system”.

Pro-Israel influence in British schools

Over the past decade, the Department for Education and British government ministers have issued warnings to headteachers, teaching staff and local authorities over how Palestine is approached in schools.

These interventions have often come after lobbying from pro-Israel groups such as UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI), the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Community Security Trust (CST).


'Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not'

- Gary Spedding, political consultant on Israel-Palestine


In 2021, the BBC removed a seven-part series of educational videos about Palestine from its GCSE Bitesize platform - a free classroom resource for teachers - following pressure from UKLFI. 

Former Conservative education secretaries Gavin Williamson and Gillian Keegan both formally instructed headteachers to ensure “political impartiality” when it came to discussions on Israel-Palestine in schools. 

“Palestine is viewed as a partisan issue triggering school neutrality, but Zionism and Israel are not,” Spedding told MEE. “Meanwhile, the activities of pro-Israel advocacy organisations, operating in and having access to UK schools, do not receive an equivalent level of UK government or institutional scrutiny,” he said. 

A plethora of pro-Israel groups, including StandWithUs UK, United Jewish Israel Appeal and JNF UK provide educational resources, speakers and trips to Israel for British students and teachers.

StandWithUs has said that it helps students “stand strong in the face of antisemitism and anti-Zionism”, while the JNF allows them to “explore Israel” and offers “workshops on Zionist history”.

“Israel advocacy organisations try to argue their presence in the school system is necessary to counter rising antisemitism and anti-Zionism in schools,” Spedding said.

“But our educational unions have noted that the resulting imbalance leaves teachers highly anxious about covering topics related to Palestine, answering pupils’ questions and queries with regard to Palestine, and that traditional pro-Israel and Zionist viewpoints go largely unscrutinised by the UK government.”

“It is not merely important to protect the space to advance vigorous criticisms of Israel’s appalling actions,” Maugham reiterated. “We think it is necessary in a moral society.”

US midterm elections 2026: Top Democrat tells Trump administration to 'lawyer up'
articles.description:
US midterm elections 2026: Top Democrat tells Trump administration to 'lawyer up'

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 14:35

        
      
    
      
    
                Robert Garcia has vowed to investigate the Trump family's business dealings. Among the issues under scrutiny could be UAE investments and a deal involving Abu Dhabi-backed investors
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US Congressman Robert Garcia convenes a hearing in West Palm Beach, Florida, 12 May 2026 (Joe Raedle/Getty Images via AFP)
                  Off
                  A senior Democrat has warned US President Donald Trump and his Republican allies to "lawyer up", vowing to investigate alleged corruption and the business dealings of the president's family following the party's midterm election victories.

Speaking to Punchbowl News on Tuesday, Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would use their congressional powers to scrutinise the Trump family's financial interests.

The California Democrat said he would investigate "Trump crypto schemes" and how members of the president's family, including Jared Kushner, were "sitting on boards and getting contracts".

"Anyone who has been in bed with the Trumps" would have "no choice but to respond to our questions", he said.

Hours later, Garcia issued a blunt two-word warning: "Lawyer up."
  
    



  



Garcia has previously pledged to investigate what he called the "Trump Crime Family", as well as corporate corruption, alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the handling of the Epstein files.

Among the issues likely to attract scrutiny are the Trump family's lucrative business relationships with foreign investors and government-linked figures, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.

In January 2025, four days before Trump's inauguration, UAE-backed investors agreed to pay $500m for a 49 percent stake in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Trump's sons, Donald Trump Jr and Eric Trump.

The investment was backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE's national security adviser and brother of the country's president.

According to the Wall Street Journal, $187m of the initial payment went to entities linked to the Trump family, while $31m went to companies associated with Steve Witkoff, Trump's Middle East envoy and a co-founder of the venture.

Conflict of interest?

The deal raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, particularly after the Trump administration subsequently approved the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips to the UAE, easing restrictions imposed under former President Joe Biden.

A separate deal involving Abu Dhabi-backed investors also brought World Liberty Financial under scrutiny.
  
    



  



In May 2025, MGX, an investment firm backed by Abu Dhabi, announced a $2bn investment in cryptocurrency exchange Binance, using World Liberty's USD1 stablecoin to facilitate the transaction.

While MGX was the investor and Binance the recipient, the use of USD1 potentially generated interest income and other commercial benefits for World Liberty through the assets backing the stablecoin.

The arrangement attracted further scrutiny after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao was pardoned by Trump in October 2025, after pleading guilty in 2023 to violating US anti-money-laundering requirements.


  

  US midterm elections 2026: Democrats sweep House and Senate in major rebuke to Trump
    Read More »


According to a June 2026 report by Democratic staff on the Senate Banking Committee, at least 10 Trump administration policy actions benefiting the UAE followed investments in Trump family cryptocurrency ventures. 

Trump's family and close associates have also established lucrative financial relationships with Saudi Arabia, raising further questions about potential conflicts of interest.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and former senior White House adviser, secured a $2bn investment from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) for his private equity firm, Affinity Partners, after leaving the first Trump administration.

The fund is chaired by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, widely known as MBS, with whom Kushner developed close ties during his time in the White House.

The Trump Organisation has also pursued property and licensing ventures across the Gulf, including projects in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Oman. These include luxury residential developments, hotels and golf resorts promoted by Trump's sons.

According to the Oversight Democrats' 2026 report, Trump and his family are believed to have generated $2.25bn in realised profits from digital currency ventures and other foreign-linked payments. The figure rises to as much as $9.72bn when estimated unrealised wealth is included.

Speaking ahead of Tuesday's election, Trump indicated that he would consider issuing pre-emptive pardons to himself and his aides if they faced investigations led by Democrats.

"I would if needed to," he told The Post's Pod Force One host Miranda Devine.

"I would not even think about it. I'd do it."

articles.title: Inspired by UK sanctions on Israel, US Democrats want to work with Labour
articles.description:
Inspired by UK sanctions on Israel, US Democrats want to work with Labour

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Peter Oborne
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:47

        
      
    
      
    
                A source told MEE that informal talks are already taking place between Democrats and the Burnham government
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband attends a panel discussion during the Warsaw Security Forum in Warsaw, Poland on 13 October (AFP)
                  Off
                  As US President Donald Trump reels from Tuesday night’s election wipeout, victorious Democrats are praising British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for inspiring new US policies towards Israel.

Democrats have told MEE that they plan to take advantage of their new hold over Congress to introduce sanctions aimed at settlers in the occupied West Bank, which would be in line with British sanctions introduced last month.

There is also talk on both sides of the Atlantic of reviving the traditional alliance between Labour and Democrats as the 2028 presidential election approaches. 

One source told MEE that informal talks are already taking place between Democrats and the Burnham government amidst expectations of a “strong relationship between a progressive Democratic president and a progressive UK prime minister”.

Democrat sources told MEE they watched British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Miliband break with Keir Starmer’s foreign policy towards Israel - and noted how popular it has been in Britain.
  
    



  



Even before last night’s momentous results, some Democrats have been publicly calling for the US to copy Labour’'s sanctions policy.

Texas Congressman Joaquin Castro described Miliband’s sanctions announcement as “a step in the right direction”. 


  

  Exclusive: Miliband set on sanctions regardless of Israel election outcome as officials try to weaken measures
    Read More »


He denounced settlement expansion as a “land grab carried out through violence and terrorism” before calling on the US to follow Britain’s lead.

Congressman Ro Khanna, who was held at gunpoint by settlers in the West Bank last summer, praised the UK’s “important moral step”. 

Matt Duss, a Washington Middle East expert with strong links to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, told MEE on Tuesday night that “seeing key allies taking these steps gives a real boost to colleagues in the US”. 

He added that, “A new class of progressive Democrat is coming into Congress who wants to support Palestinian rights.”

Democratic member of Congress, Greg Casar, has already urged a US ban on trade with the settlements.

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, meanwhile, declared that “Congress can and must act”.

'It is time' 

Emily Thornberry, the chair of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Select Committee, told MEE that if "brave and thoughtful leaders such as Reps Khanna, Casar and Castro are put into a position to develop US policy toward Israel and the occupied territories, real progress could be made."

Thornberry added: “I would recommend what we have done [on Israeli settlements] as a model, and I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this in the near future.”

In a sign that the Democrats have been inspired by Britain, 19 Senate Democrats - including Castro and Casar - introduced legislation in late September to sanction people or companies facilitating settlement construction as part of the Israeli government’s E1 plan.

The plan involves building thousands of new housing units between Jerusalem and the existing West Bank settlement of Maale Adumim, 7km east of the city. It would effectively cut the West Bank in half, making a Palestinian state unviable.

Congresswoman Madeleine Dean, one of the lawmakers behind the sanctions bill, said when it was unveiled: “It is time that the United States joined our allies - such as the United Kingdom, France, and Canada - in taking action to help preserve dignity and self-determination for the Palestinian people, which is essential for progress toward peace.”
  
    



  



Both the Sunak and Starmer governments pursued a general policy of alignment with the US. Then came Burnham’s startling break with the Trump administration over Israel, with Britain leading middle-ranking powers including France and Canada in sanctioning settlements in September.

This bold move opened up a new interest in Britain from the US Democrats, who have emerged victorious in the American midterms this week.


'I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this [policy towards Israel] in the near future'

 - Emily Thornberry, Foreign Affairs Select Committee chair


Polls have shown most of the British public, including a narrow majority of Conservative voters, supported the sanctions package.

Democrats are hoping to distance themselves from former US President Joe Biden’s support for Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza. 

With high-profile Democratic candidates critical of Israel - in particular Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who was relentlessly attacked by Trump but endorsed by former Democratic President Barack Obama - storming to victory in the midterms this week, the appetite within the Democratic Party to take a tougher stance on Israel is nearly certain to increase.

This may especially be so if Trump now launches a fresh assault with Israel on Iran - which the midterm results indicate most Americans do not support. 

In some ways, the burgeoning alliance between the Democrats and Labour recalls the close ties built up between US President Bill Clinton and Tony Blair before he became prime minister in 1997.

The relationship between Harold Wilson and Lyndon Johnson in the 1960s is another example.

A close relationship between the Democrats and Labour would therefore mark a return to traditional British foreign policy, which has been strongly tied to the United States.

articles.title: Israeli army ends 11-day Hebron raid after looting and vandalising Palestinian homes
articles.description:
Israeli army ends 11-day Hebron raid after looting and vandalising Palestinian homes

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Fayha Shalash
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 14:24

        
      
    
      
    
                Residents return to damaged houses stripped of valuables as military assault leaves hundreds displaced, businesses destroyed and West Bank city facing millions of dollars in losses
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A Palestinian man looks on as he assess the damage to his home after the Israeli military ended an assault in Hebron in theoccupied West Bank, 2 November 2026 (Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)
                  Off
                  For 11 days, Abbas Mujahid imagined returning home. He had no idea when that might be.

Israeli soldiers had forced him and his family of seven to leave the house in Hebron in the occupied West Bank last month. 

Their home is in the al-Jalda neighbourhood of Hebron, the focus of an Israeli military assault that began on 23 October and ended on Monday.

During the attack, hundreds of Palestinian families were displaced by Israeli forces. Major roads and streets were closed, the city’s entrances sealed, and a total blockade imposed. Commercial shops were raided, while industrial facilities were vandalised or demolished.

The assault caused extensive damage to residential neighbourhoods, businesses and infrastructure. Hebron now faces the daunting task of assessing the destruction, clearing debris and reviving an economy brought to a standstill by the blockade.
  
    



  



When Mujahid and his family finally returned, they found their home severely damaged and vandalised.

“We found all the wooden doors, as well as the main iron door, torn off their hinges,” he told Middle East Eye. 

“The gypsum decorative elements were completely smashed, the light fixtures broken, and our clothes and belongings scattered all over the house.” 

According to Mujahid, soldiers had also left human excrement throughout the house. Window frames had been ripped out, apparently in acts of deliberate destruction.


'My only ‘guilt’, the only reason my facility was demolished, is that I am Palestinian'

- Iyad al-Qawasmi, Hebron business owner 


During their displacement, Mujahid had tried to prepare his children for the possibility that their home, particularly their bedrooms, might be badly damaged. But nothing could spare them the shock of seeing the destruction first-hand.

“I have begun bringing in workers to repair the house, its walls, and its doors, at a cost estimated in the tens of thousands of shekels. Yet, the very fact that we have returned outweighs any sense of the damage caused,” he said.

The economic toll has been equally severe. According to estimates by the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, direct losses exceeded 12 million shekels a day (around $3.8m). A total of 327 commercial and economic establishments were shut down, 15 facilities destroyed and around 1,350 people lost their livelihoods.

The humanitarian impact was also substantial. On 30 October, Unicef reported, citing Hebron Municipality figures, that 483 families had been displaced by Israeli forces and restrictions on the city. They comprised 4,304 people, including 1,845 children.

Heavy losses

The military incursion came after a shooting by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron. The two Palestinians were also killed in the fire exchange. 

Israel has been accused of collective punishment with its response, which included mass displacement and demolitions. 

At least 15 homes and facilities were demolished, including three residential properties. Two belonged to the Palestinians who carried out the shooting attack.

Destruction extended beyond demolitions, with private property, household possessions and the contents of commercial establishments also damaged. Business owners and their employees were left facing mounting losses.

Among those affected was Iyad al-Qawasmi, who owned a used vehicle parts business in Farsh al-Hawa, an area where several factories and commercial shops were demolished on 23 October.
  
    



  



Israeli soldiers raided his three-dunum facility, which housed 600 used vehicles, and gave him one hour to evacuate before its demolition.

When Qawasmi asked for a written demolition order, rather than a verbal instruction, soldiers told him an Israeli court had issued the decision and that he had to comply.

  
  
      



    People check the damage after Israeli machinery demolished a Palestinian building near Hebron in the occupied West Bank, 3 November 2026 (Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)
  







He said he had received no prior notice. Since opening the business in 2016, he added, the facility had never been raided, apart from one incident in which surveillance cameras were confiscated.

Qawasmi brought in a bulldozer in an attempt to salvage what he could within the limited time. But several bulldozers belonging to the Israeli army and settlers then entered the site.

They seized at least 400 vehicles, along with other equipment.

“On top of my losses, which exceed 2.5 million shekels ($790,000), they confiscated the vehicles and stole the property I had inside the facility,” he said.
  
    



  



Days later, Israeli bulldozers returned and demolished the facility, reducing it to rubble. The destruction was so complete that the mountains of Halhul, previously obscured by the site, are now visible through it.

Qawasmi remains barred from accessing the land, leaving him unable to retrieve equipment or recover any belongings.

The business employed at least ten people, all of whom supported their families. Its destruction has therefore cut off the income of ten households, affecting at least 70 Palestinians.

“My only ‘guilt’, the only reason my facility was demolished, is that I am Palestinian. The facility is not even located near the site of the shooting incident,” he said.

The road to recovery

Relevant authorities have begun surveying the damage, but rebuilding what was destroyed and restoring normal life will take considerable time and resources.

Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari said the full extent of the damage to private property is still being assessed and documented.


  

  ‘We left with heavy hearts’: Israel’s assault displaces thousands in Hebron
    Read More »


He said the destruction went beyond structural damage. Residents had reported the theft of gold jewellery, cash and personal belongings, as well as broken doors and damaged household contents. 

“A government committee has been formed to assess these damages. Engineers are currently visiting the affected homes to conduct surveys and document the losses, in order to determine the exact scale of the destruction,” he said.

Damage to municipal facilities and utility networks is estimated at around six million shekels (around $1.9m), al-Jabari added.

The losses include damaged streets, pavements, water and electricity lines, as well as municipal equipment, machinery and networks across the city.

During the assault, the municipality managed the emergency through its response committee, staff and equipment. But restoring normal life and repairing the damage will take time.

“Restoring the city to its normal state and repairing the damage it sustained will require at least a month,” he said.

Burnham pledges Middle East de-escalation push after US midterms

    
    

        
    
                UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says ending the Middle East conflict is essential to easing pressure on household budgets, pledging to pursue de-escalation after the Democrats secured control of Congress.

Responding to a question about whether the election outcome could make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham said: “Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.

“That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves. But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.”

Pressed on the risk of further fighting following the vote, he said: “Well, I’ll be working for de-escalation to make it very clear. You know, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again.”

articles.title: Police urged to investigate London event advertising settlement-linked Israeli agency
articles.description:
Police urged to investigate London event advertising settlement-linked Israeli agency

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Imran Mulla
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:23

        
      
    
      
    
                Activists protested at the World Travel Market event, which began on Tuesday and is advertising the Jerusalem Development Authority
                      
                  
                  

  


                  A line of police wait to move in as protesters gather around the corner in support of the Palestine Action activist group outside the Supreme Court in central London on 4 November 2026 (AFP)
                  Off
                  The Metropolitan Police have been urged to investigate the participation of an Israeli agency involved in the construction of illegal settlements at an international travel event in London.

MEE revealed last week that the World Travel Market (WTM) event this week, which faced a pro-Palestine protest on Tuesday and will continue until Thursday, was set to feature a stand run by the Israeli government's tourist office.

The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP, a UK-based legal group, sent a letter to the Met Police's war crimes team on Tuesday demanding the "urgent investigation and consideration of preventative measures in relation to the reported participation of the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA), through its tourism platform iTravelJerusalem, at World Travel Market (WTM) London".

Activists with the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) protested next to Israel's stand on Tuesday, holding a banner reading "Every settlement is a war crime".

Video footage showed two activists being physically removed from the event by security guards.
  
    



  



Ryvka Barnard, the deputy director of the PSC, told MEE: "The Israeli state's presence at the World Travel Market in London is an utter disgrace. 

"In September, when the foreign secretary acknowledged that Israel's occupation is illegal, he said he would ban the advertising of illegal settlements. But that's exactly what's happening here. 

"This is now a test for the Labour government. Will it stick to its word, intervene to shut down this stall and call for criminal investigations into its organisers, or will it reveal that those were just empty words?"

Will it stick to its word, intervene to shut down this stall and call for criminal investigations into its organisers, or will it reveal that those were just empty words?"

The Israeli stand is shared by numerous Israeli companies and organisations, including "iTravelJerusalem", which promotes tourism in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and is managed by the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA).

The JDA, a statutory agency of the Israeli government and the Jerusalem municipality, carries out development initiatives across Jerusalem and has been heavily involved in the construction and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements on occupied Palestinian territory.

Since 2023 the JDA has a contract with Finn Partners, a global marketing agency, to advertise Jerusalem as a tourism destination in Britain.
  
    



  



'These circumstances warrant urgent investigation'

The ICJP's letter to the Met Police, seen by MEE, says: "Of particular concern is the commercial relationship between the JDA and WTM London... including the possibility that the organisers may receive exhibition fees or derive other financial benefits from the participation of an agency reportedly implicated in settlement related activities.

"We consider that these circumstances warrant urgent investigation into potential offences."

MEE has asked the Met Police and WTM for comment.


  

  Exclusive: London event advertises Israeli agency building illegal settlements
    Read More »


This comes after 15 MPs wrote to the British government on Monday calling for "urgent action" on the event.

The MPs demanded that the government "contact the organisers of WTM London and require the removal of exhibitors and promotional material where their participation would facilitate or promote illegal Israeli settlements".

Last month, the British government recognised Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory as illegal and announced comprehensive sanctions on Israeli settlements.

According to a 2025 report by the Office of the European Union Representative for the West Bank and Gaza Strip, the JDA planned "for the eviction of the Umm Haroun compound - home to approximately 40 Palestinian families - and the construction of a 320-unit settlement" in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood. 

In 2020, a JDA project to build a cable car in Jerusalem, which would involve the uprooting of trees and displacement of infrastructure including water, sewage and telecommunications, was approved by the Israeli government.

The JDA also plans to build a large settlement housing project next to the Palestinian community of Beit Safafa in East Jerusalem.

Hussam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to Britain, said in response to MEE's report last Thursday: "Next week Israeli companies guilty of ethnic cleansing will be platformed at [WTM London]."

Zomlot added: "The UK government must now turn their words into action: enforce these commitments and ensure those complicit in illegal occupation and settlements face real consequences."

articles.title: Israel's Shin Bet arrests activist amid incitement over Palestinian electoral gains
articles.description:
Israel's Shin Bet arrests activist amid incitement over Palestinian electoral gains

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:33

        
      
    
      
    
                Abu Shahadeh's detention comes amid accusations that Netanyahu’s government is seeking to undermine election results following a strong turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Abu Shahadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was arrested by masked officers who stormed his house at midnight (Provided)
                  Off
                  Israeli security forces arrested prominent Palestinian political activist and journalist Abd Abu Shahadeh on Tuesday and took him to an undisclosed location, according to news outlet Arab48.

Abu Shahadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was taken from his home in Jaffa around midnight.

Around 15 security personnel, including masked officers, stormed the house, arresting Abu Shahadeh in front of his two children. They also seized electronic devices and several books.

The forces refused to disclose the reasons for his arrest or reveal which authority had taken him away.

Police later confirmed that the case was under investigation by the Tel Aviv Central Unit and Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency. A court subsequently issued a publication ban, citing a “security-related investigation”.
  
    



  



The arrest comes amid a wave of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel following their record voter turnout and electoral gains in last week’s elections.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party claimed the elections had been “stolen” by Palestinian parties, citing allegations of minor electoral fraud.

Opposition figures have accused Likud of attempting to undermine the election results by exaggerating the allegations.

Palestinian-led parties denied the allegations. 

Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the election results on Wednesday, saying it had found no evidence of irregularities that undermined the integrity of the election or affected the outcome.

Despite this, Shin Bet chief David Zini, an ally of Netanyahu, was seeking to question the leaders of Palestinian-led parties under caution.

Those targeted included United Arab List leader Mahmoud Abbas, Ta’al leader Ahmed Tibi and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.
  
    



  



According to Haaretz, this was despite police and prosecutors having yet to see evidence supporting the allegations of electoral fraud involving the Palestinian vote.

Attempt to 'steal' elections 

Sami Abu Shehadeh said on Wednesday that Abd Abu Shahadeh’s arrest formed part of an effort by Netanyahu and Zini to “steal the elections”.

“Abd’s arrest is part of a broader campaign of arrests, interrogations and threats against political activists, designed to undermine the election results through the weaponization of the police and the Shin Bet,” the politician said.

“None of this will change one simple fact: Netanyahu lost the election, thanks to Arab citizens who turned out in massive numbers and kicked him out.”

He described the “abduction” as a serious crime but said it would not deter Palestinian citizens.

“we will not be intimidated, and we will not let them steal the election,” he added.

Abd Abu Shahadeh heads the elected Islamic Council in Jaffa and is a member of the editorial board of the Arab 48 news website.

He is also a regular contributor to Middle East Eye’s opinion section.

articles.title: ‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel
articles.description:
‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Amara Sophia Elahi
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:11

        
      
    
      
    
                The WMA maintains Israel's membership despite allegations of Israeli doctors' involvement in torture and complicity in the Gaza genocide
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Medics from the IMA Out! campaign protest outside the World Medical Association General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, on 10 October 2026 (IMA Out!) 
                  Off
                  The World Medical Association (WMA) is facing strong criticism for refusing to suspend the Israeli Medical Association (IMA), despite documented allegations of complicity by Israeli doctors in the torture of Palestinian detainees and abuses committed in Gaza.

A petition signed by 6,500 medical personnel from the IMA Out! campaign, a coalition of health advocacy groups, was presented to the WMA General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, last month, calling on the international body to expel the IMA.

Hundreds of doctors also took part in protests as the General Assembly was convening, with some carrying a shroud bearing the names of 18,000 Palestinian children who have been killed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Doctors argue that the IMA has failed to uphold core standards relating to medical ethics, and that they are complicit in serious violations of human rights against Palestinians, including failing to penalise Israeli doctors who may have overseen the torture of Palestinian detainees and the deaths of Palestinian healthcare workers in Israeli prisons.

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), a group seeking justice for war crimes, crimes against humanity and human rights violations committed by Israel against Palestinians, also filed a complaint last month to the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging it to investigate whether Israeli doctors, as well as the IMA and officials from Israel’s ministries of health and defence, have been involved in the torturing of Palestinians.
  
    



  



It is the first time that a WMA member has been referred to the ICC.

Dr Jonathan Fluxman, a retired British GP of Jewish heritage and organising member of the IMA Out! campaign, attended the protests in Rotterdam.

“Both the WMA and IMA are refusing to investigate multiple reports by numerous human rights agencies that were sent directly to them relating to the torture and murder of healthcare workers,” he told Middle East Eye.

“This goes back 30 years - the WMA has been burying reports about Israeli torture.

“They are behaving in the same way as the US and British governments, by allowing Israel to get away with a genocide. In my view, the WMA is complicit in the IMA’s involvement in this.”

‘Carte blanche’ to Israel

Dr Fluxman believes that the WMA should immediately initiate an investigation into the potential involvement of IMA members in the torture, abuse and deaths of Palestinian detainees.

“This is about defending medical principles and the application of them,” he said.
  
    



  



“It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics, and we understand that a number of national medical associations remain very concerned about the situation.”


‘It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics’

- Dr Jonathan Fluxman, retired British GP


The WMA was established in 1947 to uphold medical ethics following the Second World War, after doctors from Nazi Germany were found to have participated in war crimes.

One hundred and eighteen countries are currently represented within the international body.

Each member country must adhere to WMA codes of practice, including its 1975 Declaration of Tokyo, which states that doctors must not participate in torture and have a duty to call it out.

The last time an association was suspended was in 1976, when South Africa was blocked from attending two general assemblies due to doctors being complicit in torture during the apartheid.

The first attempt to hold the IMA accountable for the alleged participation of Israeli doctors in the abuse of Palestinian detainees came in 2009, when 725 physicians from 43 countries presented findings by human rights groups to the WMA, which that year was holding its general assembly in Tel Aviv.

At the time, the president of the IMA, Yoram Blachar, was also president of the WMA - he rejected allegations that Israeli medics were complicit in torture, describing them as defamatory.

In 2016, 71 UK-based doctors again urged the WMA to suspend the IMA, but it refused.

The Israeli association represents over 90 percent of doctors in Israel. Its current president, Zion Hagay, chairs the WMA’s socio-medical affairs committee, while its chief executive officer advocate, Leah Wapner, serves in several advisory roles, including on the WMA’s finance and planning, socio-medical affairs, and medical ethics committees.

Dr Fluxman believes that the international body is protecting the IMA.

“What has 30 years of inclusion and dialogue led to? Things have got worse, and the IMA has been given carte blanche to do whatever it wants,” he said.

Around 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed by Israel since October 2023.

South African push to expel IMA

The call for the IMA to be suspended from the WMA was led by the South African Medical Association (Sama) last year.
  
    



  



Sama’s motion failed to secure the majority that was needed to get the WMA to consider expelling the Israeli group. Instead, the WMA passed a resolution calling on the Israeli government to protect healthcare and health workers in Gaza, and asked all its members to issue public statements condemning attacks on hospitals and medical personnel.

The IMA has remained silent on this, however.

Dr Mvuyisi Mzukwa, the chairman of Sama, told MEE his group had decided to take its own approach against the IMA.

“We were the first medical association to formally cut ties with the IMA,” he said.


  

  How the Israeli Medical Association politicised medicine to defend genocide in Gaza
    Read More »


This was followed by the British Medical Association and the Turkish Medical Association.

“We also withdrew from the WMA’s Taipei Working Group on ethics because it is chaired by an Israeli medic. It is hugely problematic that the IMA is part of the WMA’s leadership structures, given the allegations surrounding them,” Mzukwa said.

“As a world body, the WMA’s name is being tarnished by the presence of the IMA, and they should have suspended them until these controversies are resolved.

“It is a huge indictment on the WMA. The international body must be clear about the principles it stands for.”

Dr Mzukwa explained that he had been planning to arrive earlier at this year’s General Assembly in order to rally other members of the WMA to join the call for the IMA to be boycotted.

However, he and most of his South African colleagues could not attend because of visa issues.

“I had applied on time, but for some reason the visa ended up being sent to Pretoria rather than Durban, where it usually goes, and there was no way I could have collected it in time for the General Assembly,” he said.

“I have my suspicions about why this might have happened. I was planning to give a speech at the General Assembly and was prepared to put my head above the parapet to call for the IMA to be expelled.

“It’s not beyond the realms of possibility that there could have been some intel on me to try to prevent me from attending.”

MEE contacted the Netherlands’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment but received no response by the time of publication.

Mzukwa has been vocal in his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. His stance aligns with that of the South African government, which brought a case to the International Court of Justice in 2023 accusing Israel of committing genocide.

Dr Mzukwa also told MEE that Sama, the IMA and the WMA had held a meeting at the end of July about the case of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, a Palestinian paediatrician and former head of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, who has been detained by Israel since December 2024 and subjected to brutal beatings.

“We raised concerns about the lack of access to Dr Abu Safiya, the denial of medical treatment for him and uncertainty around his condition,” Dr Mzukwa explained.

“The IMA told us they had requested the Israeli authorities to carry out medical examinations and allow external physicians into the prison where Dr Abu Safiya is being held, but we weren’t shown any evidence to support this - this was a red flag for us.”

‘A buttress of the Israeli state’

Derek Summerfield, an honorary senior lecturer at King’s College London who has researched and campaigned on the psychiatric impact of the detention and torture of Palestinian prisoners in Israel, has been calling on the WMA to expel the Israeli association for almost two decades.

“We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out,” he told MEE.


‘We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out’

- Dr Derek Summerfield, King’s College London


“There is a long-established body of evidence on Israeli doctors’ complicity in torture suites, and these days they are even more present there, and participate directly.

“The IMA is an example of the disgusting way in which doctors can behave - they are shielding doctors’ involved in Israel’s genocide on Gaza, and it’s outrageous that they’re a full member of the WMA.

“The IMA really is the buttress of the Israeli state.”

Dr Fluxman has also raised concerns about how the IMA’s ethical policy allows for exemptions from the WMA’s principles.

“It is their policy to allow Israeli doctors to compromise fundamental ethical principles and defer to military and security officials over the provision of healthcare and protection of health personnel,” he said.

“It also means they are in breach of the WMA’s position on medical neutrality.”

The IMA has consistently remained silent amid ongoing attacks on healthcare facilities in Gaza, as well as the targeting of healthcare workers.

In fact, it has frequently sought to challenge criticism of Israel’s actions by international medical associations.  


  

  Palestinian bodies released by Israel came from infamous Sde Teiman detention centre
    Read More »


At this year’s WMA General Assembly, the IMA installed banners outside the convention, calling on medical associations not to boycott them and asking them to remember the 7 October 2023 attacks.

In November 2023, IMA’s president, Professor Hagay, refused to call for a ceasefire and justified Israeli military strikes on hospitals in Gaza, arguing that Hamas fighters needed to be “rooted out of terror bases”.

That month, 81 Israeli doctors signed a letter supporting the bombing of hospitals, something which the IMA refused to condemn, contravening WMA principles on the protection of healthcare settings and health workers.

Furthermore, Dr Liav Goldstein, a senior member of the IMA’s ethics bureau and chief medical officer of the Israeli Prison Service, has approved the starvation diet imposed on thousands of Palestinian prisoners after 7 October by the national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir.

The IMA’s attempts to safeguard the reputation of the Israeli state were also laid bare when in May 2024, Hagay wrote to the Israeli Prison Service about the death in prison of Dr Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the orthopaedic department at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

After a highly critical British Medical Journal article about the circumstances surrounding Dr Al-Bursh's death, Professor Hagay wrote: “We would appreciate any information that could help us refute this claim, which, needless to say, causes significant harm to Israel’s standing and image worldwide.”

Torture camp

Whistleblowers from Sde Teiman, an Israeli military base in the Negev desert that was converted into a detention camp at the start of the Gaza genocide, have documented the systemic abuse and torture of Palestinian detainees there, including the denial of medical treatment by Israeli medics.

Accounts describe prisoners being held naked, shackled and forced to wear nappies instead of being allowed to use a toilet.

Some have also had to undergo amputations, often without anaesthesia.


'The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table'

- Dyab Abou Jahjah, Hund Rajab Association


The centre has been used to detain thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, the majority of whom are civilians, including healthcare and humanitarian workers, who are being held under the so-called “unlawful combatants” law, which has been used to strip detainees of basic legal protections and enable their detention without charge or trial.

Several individuals have died while being held there.

IMA ethics board director Yossi Walfisch dismissed accusations of ill-treatment and said prisoners at the camp were receiving “appropriate medical care”.

Dr Al-Bursh was held at Sde Teiman before being taken to Ofer Prison, where he died. While in prison he was brutally beaten, tortured and repeatedly raped, according to testimonies of released Palestinian prisoners who had met him.

The Hind Rajab Foundation said evidence shows that medical participation in torture and abuse at the camp was structural.

Dyab Abou Jahjah, director general at HRF, said: “Israeli physicians abandoned their neutrality when they agreed to treat patients in chains and erase what was done to them.

“The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table.”

If IMA members are found to be complicit in this, it would violate the WMA’s code of practice, values and guidelines, as well as international humanitarian law, Abou Jahjah said.

The WMA told MEE: “Inclusion sits at the core of the WMA's identity. Patients remain our focus, alongside the protection of health personnel, including physicians, wherever they serve.

“Our members, including the Israeli Medical Association, regularly call out injustices and violations of medical neutrality even when their own governments are involved.”

MEE also contacted IMA but received no response by the time of publication.
