articles.title: How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger
articles.description:
How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Elis Gjevori
 on 
Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:09

        
      
    
      
    
                Rival gas projects with Morocco and growing Emirati influence in the Sahel drive Algeria’s move to break with its non-intervention doctrine
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tiani and Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune at a meeting on 16 February 2026 in Algiers (Algerian Presidency)
                  Off
                  An Algerian military convoy arrived in Niger last Friday, marking the country's first deployment of forces abroad since 1973, when it supported Egypt in its war against the Israeli occupation of the Sinai peninsula.

The deployment marks a major departure from Algeria’s longstanding policy of principled non-intervention. It follows Algiers’ decision to send four fighter jets to Niger on 30 August to thwart an attempted coup against President Abdourahamane Tiani.

Although the North African state opposed the 2023 coup that brought Tiani to power, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune now appears willing to offer the beleaguered leader a much-needed lifeline.

Tiani requested the deployment. Speaking on Sunday, Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti said the troops would protect economic infrastructure and oil facilities belonging to Algerian companies.

Algeria is “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, Boulghiti added.
  
    



  



Retired senior Algerian diplomat Amar Belani offered a clue to Algiers’ thinking in an article published in October.

Belani described growing instability in the Sahel, including Niger, as part of a “destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies”.

Continuing instability in Niger would “directly threaten Algerian interests” and hinder the Nigeria-Niger-Algeria trans-Saharan gas pipeline project, he added.

Security imperative

Zine Ghebouli, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told Middle East Eye that the situation in the region “is imposing new security imperatives on Algiers and the necessity to secure its strategic interests, particularly in the energy sector”.

This evolving regional situation includes an increasingly strong presence of the United Arab Emirates, with which Algeria severed diplomatic relations in September after “exhausting all means to preserve bilateral relations”.


'Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive'

- Zine Ghebouli, visiting fellow, ECFR


The Algerian foreign ministry said it had repeatedly warned Abu Dhabi over its “hostile actions”, devoting significant effort to “drawing the attention of the Emirati side and warning it of the grave consequences that may result from its regrettable and unjustified behaviour”.

“Despite these numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates has persisted in these actions, which have reached a point where they can no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, or remain unanswered,” the statement added.

“The fact that Algiers took the plunge to break relations proves that Emirati manoeuvering was deemed by Algerian authorities as explosive and irreconcilable,” Ghebouli said.

The UAE’s regional interventions and partnership with Israel have drawn growing opposition from governments across the region. Sudan broke ties with Abu Dhabi over its documented funding and fuelling of the country’s bloody civil war.

Somalia, Libya and Yemen have also accused Abu Dhabi of threatening their territorial integrity through its support for rival armed groups and separatist forces.


  

  Analysis: How Algeria came to treat the UAE as a national security threat
    Read More »


“For Algiers, Abu Dhabi’s diplomatic, financial and military support to several actors in the region from Libya to Sudan and the Sahel serves divisions,” Ghebouli said.

“Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive. Also, the Emirati lobbying and pressures on regional actors to expand the Abraham Accords was another point of discord,” he added, referring to the normalisation deals with Israel and Arab states, including Morocco.

In recent years, the UAE has intensively cultivated relationships with the Sahel’s military regimes through high-level diplomacy, gold trading and investment.

In May 2025, Emirati minister Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan met the leaders of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger to discuss cooperation in economic development, energy and other sectors. Mali’s government explicitly included security among the subjects discussed.

“The Sahel has long been considered as an extension of Algerian national security and Algiers now is actively acting based on that,” said Ghebouli.

“Current geopolitical shifts and all that entails in regards to rivalry with and interventions of foreign actors mean that new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s redlines,” he added.

Competing energy corridors

Eastern Libya’s de facto ruler, Khalifa Haftar, presents another concern. The UAE backs Haftar, who commands the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF).

His military expansion towards the corridors connecting Libya and Niger has heightened Algerian concerns about Emirati influence along its southern flank.


'By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis'

- Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, senior political scientist at Irsem 


“Algeria has had a poor relationship with the Haftar family for several years, and the mutiny in Niger in the last days of August illustrated it,” Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute, told MEE.

Haftar’s son Saddam supports Mahamoud Sallah, a Nigerien opponent of Tiani.

“Saddam Haftar and the Algerian state are on opposing sides,” Harchaoui said of Niger.

“That being said, observers mustn’t assume that Algeria is intervening in Libya. Its current effort is to deploy troops on Nigerien soil, so its mission relates to what happens inside Niger: maintaining security within a framework that will become clearer over the coming days and weeks,” he added.

Turkey’s rapprochement with Haftar in October could help Algeria consolidate its foothold in the Sahel. Ankara and Algiers maintain close diplomatic relations and share interests in Libya and Sudan, potentially giving Algeria a back channel to Haftar.

Rabat is also making overtures to the Haftar family, according to reports. Lieutenant General Khaled Haftar, another of Khalifa Haftar’s sons and chief of the general staff of the eastern Libyan forces, paid an official visit to Morocco last month.


  

  The Sahel, a new front in the rivalry between Algeria and Morocco
    Read More »


Separately, energy and economic interests also underpin Algeria’s approach to Niger.

Algeria’s national energy company Sonatrach, the Nigerien government and the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation are jointly developing a 4,000-km pipeline to carry Nigerian gas through Niger and Algeria and onwards to Europe.

“The troops are meant to protect energy installations, notably Sonatrach’s oil projects and the corridor of the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline”, said Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, a senior political scientist specialising in the Arabian Peninsula at Irsem in Paris and Sciences Po Lille.

Morocco is promoting a rival pipeline along an Atlantic route, drawing on the same Nigerian gas reserves to supply the same European markets.

Crucially, the UAE has agreed to support the Nigeria-Morocco pipeline financially and technically.

“Niger is the one country the overland route cannot bypass. By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis. Rabat and Abu Dhabi clearly have an interest in the Atlantic route prevailing, and Israel indirectly through its partnership with Morocco,” Dazi-Heni told MEE.

“Algeria’s traditionally cautious strategic culture” now reflects “the new strategic constraints it faces”, she added.

articles.title: Trump says US will end $4bn annual military aid to Israel in 2027
articles.description:
Trump says US will end $4bn annual military aid to Israel in 2027

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
MEE staff
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 14:15

        
      
    
      
    
                The US president said Washington would stop the payments, but US arms sales and wider defence cooperation are expected to continue
                      
                  
                  

  


                  US President Donald Trump removes his hat as he leaves after speaking at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, 2 November 2026 (Finn Gomez Getty Images via AFP)
                  Off
                  US President Donald Trump has said that his government will not give its yearly military aid to Israel starting next year due to a prior understanding he made with Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu, Reuters reported. 

Trump added that weapon sales and other forms of military cooperation would continue. 

Speaking on Fox News on Tuesday, Trump said that the two had agreed months ago to end the military aid since Israel no longer needed it.

“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping,” Trump said.

“We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it,” he added.
  
    



  



Trump said Israel would be able to purchase weapons from the United States and other countries, suggesting that the change would affect the form of assistance rather than bring an end to military ties.

“They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world,” he said.

The comments come as US politicians face growing electoral pressure over support for Israel ahead of the midterm elections. 

A June Quinnipiac University poll found that 48 per cent of American voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believed Washington was too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively, when the question was first asked in 2017. 


  

  US senator briefed on Trump's plans to restart Iran war says proposal is 'insane'
    Read More »


The United States currently gives Israel $3.8 billion a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028.

The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes.

The defence ministry of Israel stated that talks have already begun between the US and Israel on a new framework of security cooperation.

In May, the ministry had said that the two sides had begun formal talks to replace the current memorandum, with discussions focusing on joint investment in research, development and weapons production.

The suggested framework was to move the relationship from aid to a more reciprocal partnership. 

The Congressional Research Service, a non-partisan research body that advises the US Congress, said in a July report that US and Israeli officials were discussing a possible shift after 2028 away from direct military aid and towards joint programmes.

articles.title: Ariana Resources targets 2027 development decision as Dokwe feasibility work advances
articles.description: Ariana Resources PLC (AIM:AAU, ASX:AA2, FRA:4A6) managing director Dr Kerim Sener spoke with Proactive's Stephen Gunnion about progress at its 100%-owned Dokwe Gold Project in Zimbabwe, with updated resource estimates and a feasibility study moving forward. articles.title: Novo Resources builds Australian gold drilling pipeline
articles.description: Novo Resources Corp general manager of exploration Rohan Williams talked with Proactive about the company’s upcoming drilling program at the Clone prospect within the Tibooburra Gold Project in New South Wales, as well as its wider exploration pipeline across Australia. Williams said Novo is preparing to begin a 2,700-metre drilling program at Clone, following encouraging results from drilling completed in 2025. Previous work returned near-surface, high-grade intercepts including 12 metres at 5.9 grams per tonne gold and 17 metres at 2.5 grams per tonne gold. The upcoming program is designed to step out from those results and track the mineralisation down plunge, with Novo aiming to test its potential extension for another couple of hundred metres along strike. He also discussed progress across Novo’s Western Australian portfolio. Field teams have been carrying out soil sampling, rock-chip sampling and reconnaissance mapping as the company develops targets for future drilling. Novo is planning further work at Teichman, Wyloo and Egina, while the company is also awaiting the granting of tenements at Onslow before undertaking additional fieldwork and potential geophysical surveys. At Belltopper in Victoria, Novo has a potential 2,500-metre diamond drilling program planned for the first half of 2027 and is also considering strategic partners to help advance the project. Williams said investors can expect results from the current drilling program before Christmas, alongside continued project generation work focused on identifying new gold and copper opportunities. articles.title: Senegal arrests activist for protesting against Israeli participation at Youth Olympic Games
articles.description:
Senegal arrests activist for protesting against Israeli participation at Youth Olympic Games

    
    

          
      
      
        Submitted by 
Azad Essa
 on 
Tue, 11/03/2026 - 10:34

        
      
    
      
    
                Civil society group member says pro-Palestine activist's TikTok video was misconstrued as a call for violence
                      
                  
                  

  


                  Pro-Palestinian activist Amadou Sarang Diallo was reportedly arrested on Monday for a social media post (Supplied/MEE)
                  Off
                  Senegalese civil society groups are calling for the release of a pro-Palestine activist after he criticised the government for hosting Israeli athletes at the Youth Olympic Games currently taking place in the West African nation. 

Amadou Sarang Diallo, 27, was arrested on Friday after he posted a video on TikTok condemning Israel's participation in the games, activists told Middle East Eye.

The Youth Olympic Games began on 31 October and are expected to run until 13 November, and involve nearly 2,700 athletes from around the world.

It is the first Olympic event of any type to take place on the African continent. 

Eleven Israeli athletes are participating in eight sports, including boxing, athletics, judo, artistic gymnastics, fencing, and archery. 

According to reports, the Israeli athletes were met with boos at the games' opening parade.
  
    



  



According to Amidou Sidibe, the coordinator of the civil society group Club Intermediaire, Diallo was arrested about 88km outside the capital, Dakar. 

Sidibe told MEE that Diallo had said on TikTok that Israeli citizens would "never get peace in Senegal" and this was misconstrued as a call for violence.

"In [the] Wolof language it does not mean something dangerous," Sidibe said, adding that the police searched his house but "found nothing dangerous".

'Fundamental right in any democratic society'

Likewise, in a statement released on 2 November, the National Alliance for the Palestinian Cause expressed "its deep concern" over his arrest. 

"While reaffirming its commitment to respecting the laws and institutions of the Republic, the Alliance recalls that freedom of expression and opinion is a fundamental right in any democratic society," the group said, adding that the "peaceful expression of a political conviction or activist commitment cannot, in itself, justify deprivation of liberty".

On Monday, Seydi Gassama, executive director of Amnesty International Senegal, joined calls for his release. 

"Respect freedom of expression! Amadou Sarang Diallo is not violent. He has participated in several peaceful actions denouncing the genocide in Gaza, at Abdoulaye Wade Stadium during the national team's matches," Gassama wrote on X.

Senegalese activists said the arrest was a betrayal of Senegal's historic pro-Palestine position, which culminated in Dakar joining the Hague Group when it was formed in 2025. 


  

  In South Africa, municipal elections collide with solidarity for Gaza
    Read More »



The Hague Group was established to coordinate legal and diplomatic measures to hold Israel accountable for its violations of international law. 

Since the genocide began in October 2023, there have been several pro-Palestine protests in Senegal.

In February, a group made up of artists and cultural workers wrote to the government to urge it to cut ties with Israel over the genocide in Gaza, where over 74,500 Palestinians have been killed. 

“In times of crisis, the greatness of nations is revealed. Africa, having endured slavery, colonialism, and apartheid, must reject injustice and oppression,” it said.

In May 2025, Israel’s ambassador to Senegal, Yuval Waks, was forced to leave Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar after students protested against his involvement in a local conference on campus.

Students chanted “Free Palestine,” “Free Gaza” and “Israel is a war criminal" outside the venue where he was meant to deliver his remarks.
